Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When Old Man Luzu saw a monk approach, he would simply turn his back to the wall. Whenever Juzhi was asked anything, he would only raise a single finger.
Now, tell me, do these two old fellows possess any principle of the Buddha-dharma?
After a long silence, he said: 'The intent lies with the azure dragon; it does not lie with the fish.'"
Ascending the hall. Entering the room and ascending the hall; these are the pedagogical devices of the gate and courtyard. Within the trackless path, one turns it into a track.
Old Baizhang always attained "one peg"; he could say, "Drink tea, take care, and rest."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Lay it down and its traces are lost; one exerts all one's strength yet cannot lift it.
Before an inch of iron has been applied, the clashing of blades fills the ground. Even clear-eyed monks lose their grip on the essential."
Ascending the hall: "Deshan’s staff was short; Linji’s shout was low. A phrase that does not harm the meaning of things: Zhaozhou’s 'East of the Courtyard, West of the Courtyard.
Ascending the hall: "Full presentation and partial presentation; upward and downward. Cold Spring is truly tongue-tied. Why? Because the True Man..."
In the presence [of the assembly], one must not speak falsely.
Entering the hall, he cited Yunmen’s address to the assembly: "The Buddha-dharma is exceedingly abundant; it is only that the tongue is too short.
After a long silence, Yunmen said, "It is long! The Master commented: "To speak of shortness or length is to rise up and fall down by one's own hand—the lame-legged old Yunmen!"
Compassion results in fault. The road to Chang’an is level and smooth; travelers have never been barred from passing.
Entering the hall, he raised the case of Zhaozhou showing the assembly: "To be a master of our school, one must engage people with matters of the fundamental division."
The Master took up the staff and said: "Administering blows or shouting 'Ho! is not the fundamental matter. Great capacity and great function are not the fundamental matter.
A single capacity and a single environment are not the fundamental matter. Ultimately, what is the fundamental matter? Do not speak of it before those without wisdom;
it would shatter your head and split your forehead!"
He requested Master Shixi to hang the plaque. He ascended the hall and said: "In a forge, dull iron is most abundant;

at the gate of a skilled physician, the sick are most numerous. If you wish to sharpen the dull and raise the sick, you must rely on a master to bring forth the essential, formidable tongs and hammer.
Yet, one cannot help but laugh that for thirty years, Deshan never once struck a single person who was truly liberated."
Ascending the hall: The sound of autumn fills the forests and ravines; autumn rain drips upon the wutong trees. The traveler who has not yet returned stands outside the gate, drifting along the road.
Return! Return! With a body dripping with white sweat, he unloads a breeze of purity.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the Way? Zhaozhou said, "The one outside the wall.
The monk said, "I am not asking about this Way. Zhaozhou said, "Which Way are you asking about? The monk said, "The Great Way.

Zhaozhou said, "The Great Way penetrates Chang'an. The Master commented: "Zhaozhou’s Chan is on the surface of his lips. 'The one outside the wall,' 'penetrates Chang'an'—*zhù*! (a sound like a clap or a sudden realization).
"Strike! Strike! Words and speech are upright; this is not the hand of one fishing for giant turtles. It is all in vain to grasp the fishing rod. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The ancients said, 'If you only secure the root, do not worry about the branches. What do you call the root? What do you call the branches?

A pine or cypress remains green for a thousand years, yet it does not suit the tastes of the people of the age. A peony blooms red for a single day, yet the young gentlemen of the entire city [are captivated by it]."
"Intoxicated! Thus I, this mountain monk, have spoken. Is there anyone who does not agree? If there is someone who does not agree, they are my fellow student (*sahāya*).
Please explain the circumstances of this matter.
Master Baoning Yong had a verse that says: "Under the gate of the Patriarchs, human tracks cease; its depth and peril exceed ten thousand [fathoms]."
A pit seven fathoms deep; reaching down with one’s hands, one cannot avoid wasting effort. Let the green moss grow upon the temple hall as it pleases.
Look at him speaking thus—does he even have the opening to speak? As soon as it touches the lips, one falls into conceptualization. It is just like Gautama.
In the kingdom of Magadha, he sat with his room closed. What was he saying?
In the city of Vaiśālī, Vimalakīrti was teaching the Dharma-gate of Non-duality to thirty-two bodhisattvas; they were all challenged by Vimalakīrti.
When Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "What is the Dharma-gate of Non-duality? Vimalakīrti remained silent. What was he saying? At that moment—
When Linji saw Huangbo, he asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma; three times he was struck. What did Huangbo say?
As for Deshan seeing a monk enter the gate and immediately striking him, or Linji seeing a monk enter the gate and immediately shouting—what did they say?
Even so, one cannot simply silence everyone’s mouths. When has the fire of the Way ever burned anything away?
[The Master] said: "I, this mountain monk, today can do nothing but let down a single thread to speak here and there for you all. As the Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Master, said:
'When the ancients left behind a word or a phrase, if one has not yet penetrated it, it is like a wall of silver and iron.'"
Once you have penetrated through it, you will realize that the iron walls and silver mountains are none other than yourself. I dare ask you all:
have you penetrated it yet? If you wish to penetrate it, first you must take a step back and look within yourself; you must not seek outwardly.
Second, one must ensure that the warmth of practice remains continuous. Third, one must not allow poisonous influences to enter the mind.
For instance, such activities as burning incense, prostrating, reading sutras, copying characters, or studying texts—all such miscellaneous affairs are merely outward pursuits.
Today you apply yourself to the practice, yet tomorrow you slacken again; half-believing and half-doubting, half-advancing and half-retreating.

To regress is for the "warmth" not to be continuous. Even down to reciting from the *cezi* (practice manual) and casting it out from the mold—chewing on the spittle of the ancients is for poison to enter the heart.

If you wish to be free of all these various ailments, you must let go of everything with your whole being and confront the precipice. As you edge toward the precipice and edge away from it, suddenly—life.
When the root is severed, one has arrived home. There is a moment of reaching the fundamental ground.
An ancient said, "If you have not yet attained the person's head, you must first attain the point of entry. Once you have attained the person's head, do not fail the old monk.
Furthermore, another ancient said, "If you have not yet attained the person's head, you must first attain the point of entry. Once you have attained the point of entry, you must simply cast it away."
I provide this point of entry. The mountain monk says: if you have not yet attained an entry, you must attain an entry.
Once you have attained an entry, it is precisely the right time to buy straw sandals and travel on foot. Why? Studying Chan requires awakening;
having awakened, one must meet a person. If you do not meet such a person, lacking a lineage of transmission, you will merely become a self-fabricated master who, at every move, blunts his edge.

To commit such a blunder is like a monkey-man whose tail has been exposed; by the time the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, the drum will have been broken and the monkey will have fled—what use will that be?
If one awakens and meets others, every word spoken and every breath exhaled will naturally be like water entering water.
Have you not seen how Touzi Qing visited Fushan? He had a point of realization, and Fushan pointed—
He was told to go see Xianxiu, who was then the "Exquisite Penetration" (Xiù Yuán-tōng). At that time, Qing resided at Xianxiu’s quarters;
he went there and slept soundly in the main hall. Someone went to tell Xiuxiu, "There is an Elder Qing in the hall."
After eating rice gruel and rice, [Zhaozhou] was simply dozing off. Xiu said, "Wait until I go personally to examine him.
He then took up his staff and went down into the hall. Seeing Qing, he found that Qing was indeed dozing.

Xiu struck the head of the wooden board with his staff and said, "Venerable, I have no idle food here for you to eat; I am teaching you how to sleep. Qing replied, "I do not know what you are teaching me."
Jiā asked, "What are you doing? Xiù said, "Why do you not practice Chan? Qīng said, "Fine food is not for a person already full to eat.
Xiù said, "How can it be that so many people do not approve of you? Qīng said, "Even if they were to approve, what would that matter?
Xiù said, "Whom have you seen come? Qīng said, "Fúshān. Xiù said, "No wonder you are so stubborn and insolent," and then he departed.
We called out to one another and shook hands, then returned to the abbot’s quarters. One can truly know that when two people with clear eyes meet, it is utterly distinct [from ordinary encounters].
I have heard the old monk Po’an say: "The brothers of the present day do not apply themselves to their practice with full sincerity;
therefore, they see no results. When I was traveling on pilgrimage, Mi’an was residing at Wugu Mountain in Quzhou, and I was staying there."
I served as the guest prefect (*zhikè*). Upon completing my term, I went to visit Shuǐ-ān, who was serving as the head of the two corridors at Shuanglín.

"Every night I do not sleep," he said, "but walk from the eastern corridor to the western corridor, maintaining the *huátóu* (critical phrase) while practicing meditation. After walking two or three circuits, I return to the hall and strike once, looking at the brothers in the upper and lower rooms;

they are all just like rotten winter melons. Having observed them, I [thought]: [Note: The original text ends with "I looked at them" (*wǒ cù le*), implying a realization or a moment of reflection following the observation of the laxity of his fellow practitioners.]
I reflected to myself: "If I do not seize this opportunity, I shall be like these rotten winter melons in this hall;

what use would there be for a bowl? At that time, I had performed some measure of practice and could even speak within the meditation hall, yet my life-root was not severed and my mind remained ultimately unstable.
Thereupon, I left my quarters and went to Wanshou Monastery in Pingjiang, arriving before the Sangha Hall.
"Rest. At that time, it was the lamp. Zhizan resided at Wanshou; he was a "venerable elder without nostrils.
After the morning gruel, the drum was struck and he entered the room. In my heart, I deceived him and did not go into the room.
A fellow practitioner went into the room and later came to ask me, "Did you enter the room yet? I lied to my companion, saying, "I have already entered the room. Furthermore—
He then reflected to himself: "He is my fellow practitioner; I have deceived him, and my mind remains uneasy.

He gradually intended to return to the river valley, yet he wondered what would become of that. As he pondered thus, his heart grew restless and vexed. He then proceeded to the rear of the Sangha Hall.
Suddenly, he raised his head and saw the two characters "Zhao-tang" (Illuminating Hall). His long-standing doubts were instantly resolved as he ascended the steps.

At Jiangshan, he met Mian again; there was nothing in the master’s room that did not accord with him. He then took his leave to return to Sichuan. Mian personally escorted him halfway down the mountain.
Although he had never asked for a verse, the old monk took one out from his sleeve and presented it as a parting gift, saying:
"Coming ten thousand *li* southward, you, Lasa, Rush through the flowing rapids and strike the mysterious gate. The eye at the crown of your head is struck blind."
Mahesvara’s eye: going and staying are as identical as a pearl rolling on a platter. Having received the verse, he took his leave and returned to the river valley.
Later, he presided over two or three monasteries before finally residing at Wolong in Kuifeng.
At that time, a Taoist traveling south composed a letter to the Old Monk to announce his succession to the Dharma; Ma’an was then residing at Taibai, and the Old Monk was greatly pleased.
Fozhao said, "The monks from Sichuan originally possess the Way and its meaning. Fozhao added, "It would be too late for you to realize this.
This was because Miaman, throughout his life, feared the clamor of Sichuan monks and was unwilling to have many of them on the monastic roster;
whereas Fozhao delighted in Sichuan monks, as there were many of them in his hall. The Old Monk Po’an resided in Sichuan for several years.
The Monastery. Again, coming further south, this mountain monk went forth on pilgrimage. Although I went there to pay my respects, I never took up residence under him.
Later, while staying at Qionglong in Pingjiang, I finally lived within his assembly and followed him until we reached Fengshan Yang Temple, where he sent me back to the Librarian’s quarters.
There I observed the functioning of his pedagogical devices within that room, and...
His ordinary expositions were utterly unlike those of other quarters, causing people’s minds to die out. This is why I have come forth today to succeed him.
The Old Monk said: "Monks, all the responses given within the meditation room are merely products of intellectual views and conceptual understanding."
How can one fully realize this? One must go beyond words and phrases; at the moment of need, there must be a distinct wisdom that departs from the mud and water, and only then will it be attained.
Long ago, when I returned from my travels, I was traveling with a companion and stayed at a fishing lodge in Hezhou.
Among them was also a venerable elder of the former generation. When I went into his room for instruction two or three times, he refused to bring up a koan for me.
However, when my companion went into his room with me, the elder did not refuse him;
he merely tapped his knee once and said, "Try and give a turning word here. My companion remained speechless. Time after time, whenever he entered the room, it was only...
He asked him this. The traveling companion said, "I cannot bear this fellow;
time and again he asks me only this, and I have nothing with which to respond to him. You must provide a turning phrase for me; when I return, I shall apply it.
The Old Monk said, "When he asks you this again this time, simply pinch your nose with two fingers and make a 'keng' sound at him."
As soon as the sound [of the bell] fell, his companion indeed went into the room. Following the instructions of the Old Master, the Venerable One said, "Someone has misled you.
He knew that those who have attained this matter are like two mirrors; naturally, they do not deceive one another.
I urge my brothers: when practicing *gong'an* (koan), you must work at the essential point so that you may reach this state.
Only when the ground is level can it be fit for sowing grass. Once, there was a monk who visited Huìtáng. Táng asked, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "From Nánxióng Prefecture. Táng asked, "What have you come for? The monk said, "I have come to see a venerable elder.
Táng said, "Why do you not return to your hometown? The monk said, "I have come out to practice Chan; why, Master, do you [ask me to]..."
He ordered So-and-so to go back. Huitang said, "In my hometown, three coins would buy a piece of salted fish as large as a palm.
Tell me, where does Huitang’s meaning lie? Jianyuan An said, "Better to undergo eternal sinking and drifting than to ever blind the eyes of sentient beings.
Jianyuan speaking in this way is much like trying to force a square peg into a round hole.
Kong: "The others feared there might be some further depth [to this]. Later, he revealed it in the rice-room. On the Dragon Boat Festival (Duanwu), he gave a general discourse:
'To practice Zen, one must penetrate the barrier of the Patriarchs; for wondrous awakening, the path of the mind must be severed.

If the path of the mind is not severed, the barrier of the Patriarchs is difficult to penetrate. If you wish to sever the path of the mind, you must ensure that internally nothing is emitted and externally nothing is received.'"
Place it [within]. It is empty and vast. Or, when delusive thoughts arise, take up a *huatou* (critical phrase) and confront them with a precipice.
It is like brandishing a single blade of the Vajra King’s precious sword; who would dare meet its edge?
As you go back and forth over this precipice, after a long time, whenever you encounter objects or conditions, they will naturally snap with a *chui* and break with a *bao*. At that moment—
Without attachment. When you question people, there will immediately be a point of entry; thus, you will no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world.
This is called having a firm foundation; you will naturally know how to manage your own livelihood. Here at Ling Shan, we do not even need to pat our brothers on the back.
Nor do I twist or turn your brothers' words. If I see an inch, I tell you it is an inch;
if I see a foot, I tell you it is a foot; if I see a fathom, I tell you it is a fathom.
I do not deceive you by telling you that practice is difficult to perform, nor do I mislead you by telling you that practice is easy to perform. I wait for you...
To the very core and to the very bottom. One must know for oneself what is good and what is evil. Master Foyan said: "Brothers, in practicing the Way there are two kinds of faults.
The first is seeking the donkey while riding the donkey; the second is having already mounted the donkey yet refusing to dismount.

To seek the donkey while riding the donkey is to seek one's own self by means of one's own self. Having mounted the donkey yet refusing to dismount is to be caught by the mysterious and wondrous [teachings] of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

It is especially entangling; one cannot escape it. When you reach this point, if you wish to mount, you mount; if you wish to dismount, you dismount—only then do you possess the portion of true freedom.
Nowadays, Zen practitioners generally fail to have faith in themselves; they simply do not trust their elders.
It does not matter if you do not believe others; you must simply believe in what is beneath your own feet.
Only when you realize that there is this light that covers heaven and earth will each person attain emptiness—each one with their nostrils piercing the heavens.
Yet, when questioned, five out of ten do not know where it lands. Therefore, on the Dragon Boat Festival, Old Dongshan addressed the assembly, saying: "I, the old monk..."
I obtained a divine talisman of great efficacy. My first wish is that the present Emperor may live for ten thousand years;

my second wish is that the civil and military officials may always retain their posts and emoluments; and my third wish is that the myriad people may enjoy their vocations and that the winds and rains shall be harmonious.
I ordered a ghost-messenger to go throughout the four quarters of the world to announce these matters one by one. When the ghost-messenger returned, he said: "I have already gone to the four..."

Throughout the world, everyone was informed one by one until all were compliant and obedient. Only the Chan practitioners remained—those whose nostrils reach toward the heavens—and there was nothing that could be done with them.
Dongshan said, "Let us not say that you cannot do anything with them; I, too, cannot do anything with them."
Although it is thus—vast marshes conceal mountains, and principle can subdue the leopard—how is it in the end? One draws out three; two adds four.
The horns of the yellow ox point toward heaven; eight legs hang past the nose. Hurry!
As for Dongshan speaking in this way, do you all know where it lands? It is certainly not Chinese, nor is it Sanskrit. How would you say it?
Understand it! If you can understand it, then even if you were to relieve yourself on the summit of Mount Dongshan, it would not be considered out of place;
it would be just like a person from Sizhou seeing the Great Sage. What a trivial matter this is! If you cannot understand it, you must not be careless;
you must also chew it over bit by bit, from every angle, to see what principle it is that you are looking for.
It is so. Among those who practiced Chan within the volumes of scriptures, none surpassed Zhenjing Wen in penetrating to the very top and bottom and attaining great enlightenment.
When Zhenjing first began his travels as a wandering monk, he said of himself: "My realization is like a painting by Wu Daozi;
it is rendered with such lifelike precision that it is merely a painting. Therefore, I do not consider it small enough. Thus, he traveled everywhere to seek instruction from various masters. One day—
I have heard people cite a monk asking Yunmen, "Is it true that the Buddha-dharma is like the moon in the water? Yunmen replied, "In the clear waves there is no path through.
There was a point where he understood this; however, when he went to see Huanglong, their karmic conditions had not yet harmonized.

This was because although he possessed some small measure of awakening and understanding, he had not yet penetrated to the very top or the very bottom, which is why they did not harmonize. Now, the *Pudeng lu* (Universal Lamp Record) instead records [Yunmen's reply] as, "The pure [moon] in the clear waves."
There was no way through, yet there was awakening. He went to see Huanglong, but he had made a mistake all along; he simply did not realize it.
When Jingjian found that Huanglong did not accord with him, he said, "I have something good; this old fellow does not recognize me.
He then went to see Xiangcheng Shun and attained great enlightenment under Shun’s words. Upon returning to see Huanglong, he finally achieved a karmic accord and received the transmission from Xu.
Zuoxi Deng was someone who merely specialized in compiling historical records; ultimately, his vision was not correct, and thus he made errors.
Jing went to see Master Lǎoshùn, who asked, "Where have you come from? Jing replied, "From Huanglong.
Shun asked, "What sayings or phrases has Huanglong had lately? Jing said, "Lately, the local government has commissioned Huanglong..."
Elder Huangbo. Huanglong uttered a turning phrase, saying: "Reciting hymns atop the bell tower; planting vegetables beneath the bedframe.
He said, "If anyone can offer a phrase that accords with this, I shall invite them to take up residence. The senior monk Huangbo Sheng offered the phrase: "A fierce tiger sits blocking the road.
Huanglong then ordered him to go and reside at Huangbo. As he was leaving, Sheng unconsciously remarked, "Senior Monk Sheng could only offer such a [limited] phrase."
With a single turning word, Jingzhao obtained Huangbo’s dwelling; yet he had not even dreamed of the Buddha-dharma.

Under the words "Purely following," he struck his own nose until it fell out, and only then did he realize the scope of Huanglong’s application. He then returned to see Huanglong. Huanglong asked, "Where have you come from?
Jingzhao said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master. Huanglong said, "It happens that I am not here at this moment. Jingzhao said, "Where [are you]..."
Jing went off. Long said, "Tiantai was performing communal labor; Nanyue was traveling the mountains. Jing said, "If that is so, then I have attained mastery.
Long said, "Where did you buy those shoes on your feet? Jing said, "I bought them at Mount Lu for seven hundred coins.
Long said, "When have you ever attained mastery? Jing said, "When have I ever not been masterful? It turns of itself."

It rolls about like a gourd on water; it cannot be suppressed or constrained. One truly knows that when a person who has attained speaks with another who has attained, there is naturally a distinction.
Furthermore, after Sīxīn had become a monk, he resolved to travel as a wandering mendicant.
He first visited Huìtáng, who asked him: "To call it a fist is to hit against it (chù); not to call it a fist is to turn one's back on it (bèi). Sīxīn was at a loss for a response.
Sishang continued to argue forcefully, but Xuedou (Tang) eventually suppressed him. One day, as Sishang still argued insistently without ceasing, Xuedou said, "Wait, wait!
Talking about food will never satisfy one's hunger. Sishang said, "I have come this far; my bow is broken and my arrows are spent. I pray that the Master will show me his compassion."
[The Master] said, "The Dharma-gate of Peace and Bliss. Tang said, "A single speck of dust flies up and obscures the heavens; a single mustard seed falls and covers the earth.
You are simply sitting there because your conceptual understanding is too great. If you wish for the Dharma-gate of Peace and Bliss, you must first die the death of the whole mind;

only then can the mind silently receive the meaning. One day, while sitting in meditation, he suddenly heard the head of the storehouse striking the novices with a staff, like a sudden clap of thunder.
He then attained great enlightenment. Rushing out to see Huìtáng, he forgot to put on his sandals.
As soon as he saw Huìtáng, he pointed to his chest and said, "Master, everyone in the world practices Chan that can be 'attained'; I have realized Chan that can be 'awakened to.

Huìtáng said, "Having passed the imperial examination for the selection of Buddhas, how could you be contained by such words? This may be called the model of a senior practitioner engaged in Chan, my brother.
If you wish to practice Chan, you must take this as your banner before you can succeed. Do not emulate the elders of the present day;
for these elders possess but a fragmentary understanding and cannot compare to the ancients.

If you emulate the elders of the present day, you will trivialize the essential matter and fail to achieve anything of substance. Take, for example, Master Xun’s tenure at Lingyin: he was simply helpless.

Pressed from the east and squeezed from the west, driven into the corner of the meditation seat with no way to evade, one has no choice but to manifest the gateway of the Patriarchs by breaking through the mask of the face.
This is called: "Where there is no cinnabar here, red earth is taken as supreme.
Nevertheless, look at the present day; gradually even the red earth is disappearing, and we have reached the point where the grain is exhausted and only the husks remain.
The husks have long since vanished; they gradually began to eat mud and soil. To speak of this truly makes one’s heart shudder with cold.
Furthermore, my brothers who come after me must exert great courage and emerge to vindicate the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

First, you must apply your efforts to the direct shortcut; do not merely indulge in excessive knowledge and clever explanations, for you would otherwise miss the path that cuts straight through. For now—
The story of Zhaozhou washing the alms bowl is the most direct and concise. Yet many of you, brothers, understand it as being "nothing to do.
When Muzhou addressed the assembly, saying, "This is a settled case; I grant you thirty blows," how much more direct and efficient that was! Yet even so, you brothers have missed the mark.
When Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying, "Sitting inside a rice basket—there are those who would starve to death," [the meaning is] like the river water...
Drowned head-first; there are those who die of thirst. Yunmen said, "The whole body is rice; the whole body is water.
The higher the chant, the fewer the responses. How much effort has been spared! Yet you brothers do not turn your eyes toward this point; you have utterly wasted your time.
Today is the Dragon Boat Festival (Duanwu), so let us further cite one more koan before dispersing. Mañjuśrī commanded Sudhana to gather [flowers].
[Mañjuśrī] said, "Medicine. Sudhana replied, "I have surveyed the great earth; there is nothing that is not medicine. Mañjuśrī said, "If it is medicine, bring some here.
Sudhana then plucked a blade of grass and handed it to Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī held it up and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This medicine can kill a person, and it can also bring a person to life.
The Master [Yunmen] commented, "Gathering the medicine and administering the medicine—meeting thus in a single encounter."
The family: they kill people and save people without batting an eye. Pure white jade is flawless, yet it possesses a flaw. Why is this so?
If you all bring your practice to completion, you will know where the point lies.
Citing an ancient precedent, Master Mazu said: "The very mind is Buddha; neither mind nor Buddha. It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing."
The Master holds up his whisk and says: "This mind is Buddha; the sweet melon is sweet to its very core. 'Neither mind nor Buddha'; the bitter gourd is bitter to its roots.
'Neither mind, nor Buddha, nor thing'—one cuts down the cassia tree in the moon, and the clear light bursts forth at the sea gate.
If one can open the True Eye within this realm, the universe is settled upon the tip of a single hair."
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "I am a student who has newly entered the monastic community; I beg the Master for instruction.
Zhaozhou said, "Have you finished eating your congee? The monk replied, "I have finished eating my congee. Zhaozhou said, "Go wash your bowl. At these words, the monk attained realization.
The Master held up the whisk and said: "Zhaozhou used the wind to fan the fire; he did not exert much effort.
Although this monk attained awakening, he could only become a long-term provider of rice and gruel for the community. Why? You must further know that there is a higher barrier beyond."

Yunmen raised this case for the assembly, saying: "To awaken to the Way upon hearing sound, and to clarify the mind upon seeing form—when Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva went to buy a sesame cake with his money, as soon as he let go of his hand, it turned out to be a steamed bun."
The Master picks up the topic and says: "Yunmen, amidst a path of no meaning, instead opens a path of meaning. Jiangshan is not like this: 'Hearing sound, one awakens to the Way;
seeing form, one clarifies the mind. A forest of gallows and mortars; planting *lingzhi* beneath the well. This year’s peaches and plums are in full bloom;
each single fruit is worth a thousand pieces of gold."
[The Master] cited an instance where a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One, "What Dharma did you preach yesterday? The Honored One replied, "I preached the Dharma of fixedness.
He asked again, "What Dharma did you preach today? The Honored One replied, "The Dharma of non-fixedness. [The Master] said, "Why was it fixed yesterday?"
"Today is unsettled," the Honored One said. "Yesterday was settled; today is unsettled.
[The Master] picked up the point and said: "Yesterday settled, today unsettled—how great is Gautama! By means of the heterodox, he strikes the orthodox.
Furthermore, one asks: how can a begging bowl have a handle attached?"
A monk asked Master Yunmen, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen replied, "On the waters above the mountain to the east.
Later, Yuanwu offered a different response: "A fragrant breeze comes from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool."
The Master held up the whisk and said: "To see through thoroughly and to employ with intimacy—this is not without Yunmen and Yuanwu.
But as for the place where all Buddhas emerge, it takes sixty kalpas over three lifetimes."
A monk asked Nanquan, "The Master resides in the hall; with what do you point the way? Nanquan said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox;
when I rose at dawn, I had lost my fire."
The Master picks up the case and says: "Great Nanquan was so thoroughly squeezed by this monk that his hands and feet were completely exposed.
Suppose someone were to ask me, 'Master Nanshan, when you dwell in your chamber, what do you use as a guide? I would simply pull out my staff and strike him.
Why? Because gold is never sold mixed with sand."
Jingqing asked a monk, "What is that sound outside the gate? The monk said, "The sound of raindrops. [Jingqing continued as usual. The *niàn* (commentary) says:
Jingqing obstructed others with his own views; he suppressed the worthy and degraded them to the lowly, unwittingly becoming drenched in mud and water himself.
Nanshan asked a monk, "What is that sound outside the gate? He waited for him to say, "The sound of raindrops," and then granted him the recognition of possessing "one eye."
[The Master] cites the case of Guishan asking Yangshan, "Is it cold for you? Yangshan replied, "Everyone is right here.

[The Master] comments: "Everyone is right here; vast and clear, there is nothing to rely upon. Though one has a mouth, it is difficult to distinguish [the truth]. A pair of ears have been frozen through."
It is said that there was once a monk under Deshan’s assembly who stepped forward and assumed the posture of a wrestler.
Deshan said, "This impudent fellow deserves a blow from my staff."
The Master held up the whisk and said: "This monk’s child has lost its manners; Deshan’s small kindness obstructs his great kindness.

At that time, where did the white staff go? Under the gate of Nanshan, if a monk were suddenly to step forward and assume the posture of a wrestler, this old monk would have no choice but to retreat three paces.
Why? Because an old man does not rely on physical strength for his capability."
Yunmen asked a monk, "Who in the entire world can understand the Buddha-dharma? The monk replied, "The pillar.
Yunmen shouted, "This dead frog!"
The Master held up the whisk and said: "This monk has already bared his eyes; Yunmen goes further and strips away the skull-cap.
As for the Buddha-dharma, he has not even dreamed of it."
Master Chacha of Tongan asked a monk, "Do not tell anyone on my behalf that I have a kōan (in-yuan) to present to you.
As the monk made a gesture of listening, Chacha gave him a slap. The monk said, "Why did you strike me?"
An said, "I want to speak of practice.
[The Master] picked it up and said: "Old man Tongan! He was slightly ahead at first, but in the end he made people laugh to death.
Had he run into another monk, he would not have escaped suffering a poisoned hand. If it were Nanshan, when that monk asked, 'Why did you hit me?'—"
Jiā gave him another slap, whereupon [the cat] was seen with its head straight and its tail straight.
Guishan raised this up and asked Yangshan, "Let us set aside the matter of the present for a moment; how about the matter of antiquity?
Yangshan stepped forward with his hands folded. Guishan said, "That is still the matter of the present. How about the matter of antiquity? Yangshan—
He joined his palms and withdrew to the rear. Guishan said, "You have defeated me;

I have defeated you. [The Master] comments: Father and son were as harmoniously blended as water and milk—none could equal Guishan and Yangshan. Yet, when examined closely, they failed to reach the village ahead.
Later, he did not open a shop. Had he encountered Linji or Deshan, he would have struck one more blow to settle the matter once and for all.
Master Panshan addressed the assembly, saying: "The path that leads upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages;
students toil their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections. Langya Huijue commented: "All the preceding lectures and praises constitute boundless seeds of merit."
The Master held up the whisk and said: "One who possesses the eyes of the higher realm is not without Langya; yet, you must still see what Panshan was before you can grasp it.
Why? Because a person of great capacity turns within the flow of the discourse."
Baofu said, "If everyone were like this today, the Old Barbarian would have cause for hope. Changqing said, "If everyone were like this today, the Old Barbarian would be without hope.
[The Master] comments: One has hope; the other is without hope. Xu Liu carries a board and sees only one side. As for me, the mountain monk—
But that is not so. If everything were as it is today, how much effort would be spared! Thirty years from now, do not say that Nanshan has bent the crooked to make it straight.
A monk asked Dabe: "Setting aside the top and removing the bottom, I ask you, Master, to speak. Dabe said: "As soon as I open my mouth, I am wrong."
The monk said, "If that is so, then you are truly my teacher. Guishan Beicheng said, "Today you have fallen into the hands of your disciple;
you shall die. [The Master] commented:
"The wind of his coming can be discerned, yet a team of four horses cannot overtake it. Had there been no subsequent words, how could one have sought out 'Great Compassion'?"
One day, Cui Chan ascended the seat and said, "Come forth and strike! Come forth and strike! At that moment, a monk stepped forward and asked, "What about Cui Chan?
Cui Chan cast down his staff and immediately returned to his quarters.
The Master held up the case and said: "Cui Chan was greatly alarmed and acted with petty suspicion;

he oppressed an innocent person, yet he was struck by this monk with a single blow upon the crown of his head, until he was reduced to a state of total disarray. But tell me, where exactly was he disarrayed? He let out a shout."
It is said that when the Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Master, was residing at Taiping, he addressed the assembly, saying: "I, Taiping, do not understand Chan;
I have been wandering outside all along. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, I have gained nothing but a mouth.
Now, what is this mouth of Taiping? He then said himself: "Two pieces of skin—I do not even recognize them."
The Master held up his whisk and said: "The old fellow Taiping raised himself up only to topple over. Although I, Nanshan, am unworthy, I cannot help but imitate him.
I do not understand Chan; I have always been running outside. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, my tongue will not leave my mouth."
Why is it thus? This is a ready-made koan.
It is said that under Mazu’s assembly there was a monk who drew four lines with his hand and asked Mazu, "The top line is long, and the three bottom lines are short.
One must not say, "One line is long and three lines are short," for this transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
"No. "Please, Master, answer. The Patriarch drew a line with his hand and said, "One cannot say that one stroke is long and three strokes are short.
"Your answer is complete," he said. [The Commentator] remarks:
A felt gong and wooden clappers; a flute without holes. Meeting on a narrow path, the five notes and six scales have fallen into disuse within the monastic groves.
"I do not know how many years it has been. To this day, who would dare to communicate news?
Yunshan said this as a monk came to pay his respects. Yunshan rose from his seat; the monk then departed.
Yunshan remarked, "How remarkably sharp and quick-witted! The monk shouted, "To have such an eye as this—to be a Dharma heir of Linji! That is truly a great pity! Yunshan [laughed].

[The Master] said, "I simply hope that you, Ācārya, will transmit this well. The monk turned his head back; the Master then shouted and said, "With such eyes as these, you have misjudged the terminology of all quarters," and he struck him.
The Master picks up the case and says: "Yunshan and this monk—punching and kicking back and forth, their strength was equal and their power matched.
Although Yunshan’s command was carried out, how could there ever have been an eye on the end of his staff? Although this monk received the blow, in his heart he was simply not satisfied.
If anyone can discern this, Nanshan invites him to eat a bowl of plain buckwheat noodles."
An elder of former times said: "If there is even a single thread of delusion, it is indeed a single thread of delusion.
An elder of later times said: "If there is even a single thread of delusion, it is not a single thread of delusion."
The Master picks up the topic, saying: "A single staff, two people supporting it together—what joy is there in that?
Lingshan was not like this: "Is this single thread real or not? The wild man beneath the forest trees is lofty; the young lord in his brocade robes is noble."
He raised the topic of the "Gate of Wisdom" and asked the assembly, "Everyone is performing somersaults on level ground;
have you ever seen anyone perform a somersault in empty space? The monks were speechless. Yunmen spoke on their behalf, saying, "Stop jumping about."
The Master held up the staff and said: "Yunmen spoke thus, yet he has not yet managed to block the mouth of the wise.

If it were I at Lingyin, seeing him speak in such a manner, I would simply say to him: 'Today you have come out small but encountered something great. This old fellow possesses the mechanism of a spear piercing through an arrow;
even so, he is already buried a thousand fathoms deep."
When Mingzhao saw Shengguang, as soon as he stepped across the threshold, Shengguang lowered one foot. Mingzhao said, "Your tricks are exhausted.
He then shook out his sleeves and departed.
The Master held up the whisk and said: "To act in accordance with the occasion is not without its risks; yet, to seek the supreme light is still not yet possible.
Why? Because the roots are deep and wide beneath the lairs of fish and dragons, and the atmosphere is lofty at the edge of the sun and moon."
A monk asked Dongshan, “What is the Buddha? Dongshan said, “Three pounds of flax.
[The Master] comments: Do you all wish to see Dongshan? Having eyes but no ears, sitting by the fire in the sixth month.
Jingqing stood before the Sangha hall and struck the bell himself, saying, "Xuansha has reached the bottom; Xuansha has reached the bottom.
At that time, a monk came forward and asked, "What did Xuansha say? Jingqing drew a circle.
The monk said, "If you had not practiced for a long time, how would you know it was like this? Jingqing replied, "Give me back the money for my straw sandals."
The Master picks up the case, saying: "Jingqing shakes his head; this monk wags his tail. Although this is a remarkable display for the occasion, it cannot withstand Xuansha’s final word.
He then cites a monk asking Mazu Daoshi: "Beyond the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations, I pray you, Master, point directly to the meaning of the Westward Transmission."
The Master of Horses said, "I am weary today; I cannot explain this for you. Go ask Zhizang.
The monk asked Zhizang, and Zhizang said, "I have a headache today. Go ask my elder brother Hai. The monk asked Hai, and Hai said:
When I arrived here, I did not understand. A monk then asked Master Ma. The Master said, "The head of Zang is white;
the head of Hai is black. [The Commentator] says: Master Ma and Zang’s illness are of one kind. Brother Hai did not understand; he was flatly deceived face-to-face. "The head is white."
Black-headed. His words are upright and his speech is upright. Zen monks do not use their efforts in vain. When the scale is in the stars, it does not reside on the pan.
Quoting Xuedou’s verse on "Daily Diminution for the Sake of the Way": Three parts of one’s life have already passed; The single point of the numinous mind remains unpolished.
One pursues the days in pursuit of life, busily hurrying along; If one cannot turn back when called, what can be done?

The Master picks up the whisk and says: "Xuedou casually raises his hand and turns earth into gold. If you all can understand how to cast your body across [the world], then even in white robes you will pay homage as a high minister.
If this is not yet so, for the time being you will continue to emerge and submerge yourselves within the realm of conceptual consciousness."
Jiuming Zhao raised his staff to address the assembly, saying, "The wind here is somewhat stiff; let us return to a warm place to deliberate.

He then descended from the seat and returned to the abbot’s quarters. The assembly followed him there, where he remarked, "Upon reaching this warm place, you will see that everyone is nodding off," and with his staff, he struck them all at once to disperse them.
The Master held up the staff and said: "Mingzhao entered the mud and water twice; he did not fail his master.

It is a pity that at that time there was not a single monk among the assembly who could have seen through him. Ling Shan would never have followed the example of that old fellow Mingzhao by covering it over."
"How wonderful! This is a clear and lucid statement. Let it be as it is; let the ducks listen to the thunder.
The Master [Zhaozhou] himself raised the case of Yunju Yan asking Xuefeng, "Has the snow outside the gate melted yet? Xuefeng replied, "Not even a single flake remains.
What could possibly melt? The Master then said himself, "It has melted. Baofu remarked, "In any case, there was no snow to begin with."
"Adding frost. [The Master] picks it up and says: "Yunju beats the grass to startle the snake; Xuefeng opens his mouth and reveals his gallbladder;
Baofu alone ascends the high platform—yet even so, he cannot deceive the eyes of the multitude. Has the snow melted outside the gate yet? I ask you all: try to offer a turn of words."
It is related that Zhaozhou was at Nanquan’s well-house. Seeing Nanquan passing by, he grabbed hold of a pillar and stood with one foot suspended, crying out, “Save me!
Save me! Nanquan then climbed the ladder and called out, “One, two, three, four, five.
Zhaozhou then assumed a formal posture and went up to the abbot’s quarters, saying, “I thank the Master for saving me just now.”

The Master picks up the whisk and says: "Father and son are most intimately related; their mind’s eye is one and the same. Wherever they strike or encounter resistance, they penetrate to the very top and bottom.
To an onlooker, this appears merely like a child's play, yet it stirs the waters of the clear deep pool like a blue dragon."
Gushan raised his staff and addressed the assembly, saying, "Under Gushan’s gate, one must not cough. At that moment, a monk happened to cough once.
Gushan asked, "What are you doing? The monk replied, "I have a cold. Gushan said, "A cold is fine."
The Master held up the whisk and said: "This old fellow from Gushan was terrifying enough at first, yet he is laughable in the end.
Under the gate of Lingyin, you must not cough. If someone were to let out a single cough, I would ask, 'What are you doing?
When he says, 'I have a cold,' I would strike him across the spine with my staff. Why? Because unless the medicine causes a violent reaction, the disease will not be cured."

The patch-robed monk does not know how to discuss the seasons; he simply sits there in a daze, passing his life. It does not come from the past, it does not go to the future, and it does not dwell in the present.
What, then, can be called "this life"? You must know that the Yellow-Faced Old Man and the Old Barbarian with the Missing Teeth [the Buddha] are, day and night...
[The Master] conversed with the people, whispering from ear to ear: "The Iron Ox of Shanzhou is the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging. Can you all believe this?
If you can believe it, then cast off the head-rope and unload the pack-saddle; whether carrying up or down, cut everything off at once.
Let the eyes not hang upon the door, and let the mind not dwell in the profound mystery. Be directly like a withered tree on a cold cliff. One.
The Yang has not yet arisen. After the first Yang has arisen, there is no mutual interaction with anything else. One eats when hungry and drinks when thirsty;

one sits at ease and sleeps when weary. What fault is there in this? Nevertheless, even if it is thus, should one suddenly encounter a fellow who bites pigs and dogs, he will pull the sitting mat right off.

He stretches out his hairy hand. Again, how should one respond? After a long silence, he said: "Having experienced many bloody battles on the fields of sand, in the end, one's original countenance remains unchanged."
A Winter Night. The Old Barbarian came from the West, pointing directly to the human mind. The Second Patriarch sought his mind, but it was utterly unfindable.
Later generations have not heard the matter truly; they grasp at the meaning and make haphazard guesses, stumbling and bumping along until they miss the very first stroke.
They do not realize that their own nostrils hang down like a great head; they merely say, "The Yellow River is turbid from its source. Enough, enough, enough! Do not.
Hush, hush! Here at Mount Ling, there is no Chan for you to investigate and no Way for you to study. It is cold and still, dry and withered.
Tomorrow, when the first yang begins to return and the masses of yin are completely stripped away, tonight we have gathered for a short while to respond to this season.
I shall certainly not take refined gold of a hundred smeltings and sell it as mere common stone. Thus I speak.
Talk! If you were a man of true substance, you would have covered your ears and turned back from three thousand li away; even that would have been eight *ke* too late. Why?
Because you are seeking Chang’an atop the Han-yuan Palace; willow catkins are not the snow upon the heavens.
On New Year’s Eve, the golden crow hastens and the jade hare speeds. Of the three hundred and sixty days of a year, tonight marks the turning of the head.
The iron ox of Shanfu and the stone woman of Huangmei each add one year tomorrow. As for you all—how should you proceed?
Recall the final words of Master Shitou in the *Cantong Qi*: "I respectfully inform those who investigate the mystery: the light..."

Do not let the hours of the night pass in vain. If you rely on the perspective of Mount Jiangshan, then burning incense, prostrating, studying the Buddha, studying the Dharma, seeking the profound, and seeking the subtle—all of these are merely wasting your time.

Since burning incense, prostrating, studying the Buddha, studying the Dharma, and seeking the profound and the subtle are all forbidden, how should you apply your mind throughout the twelve periods of the day? If you do not know this, you cannot avoid falling into [delusion].
Within the realm of emotional consciousness, one sinks and emerges like a head bobbing in water. Therefore, Deshan addressed the assembly, saying:
"If you have no affairs within the mind, and the mind has no affairs, it will naturally be empty yet spiritual, void yet wondrous. Zhaozhou said:
"Aside from the two times for rice gruel and meals, this old monk has no other use of his mind. He also said: "All people are driven by the twelve hours; I, however, am the one who drives them."
At the twelfth hour, these two great elders made such a proclamation; what was their intention?
If you are a person with "triangular eyes," you will see through it at a single glance and walk hand-in-hand with the two elders.
If this is not yet so, remember that the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month is Little New Year’s Eve. Suddenly, when Great New Year’s Eve arrives, how will you respond? *Mò*! (Suddenly!)
[The Master] holds up his staff, strikes it once, and says: "If a person lacks far-sighted foresight, they will surely have immediate troubles.
On this year-end eve, the crow and the hare race swiftly east and west; the seasons of the year have come to an end. "Dong Ba’s cloth shirt is worn through; the turtle’s eyes are red.
Master Zhao said, "Things do not shift," yet he carries a single board and sees only one side. As for us monks—whom [can we call our own]?
Who cares about heaven? Who cares about earth? Eat to relieve hunger; open your mouth to draw breath. This year it is thus; next year it will be thus;
the year after that it will be thus; and the year after that it will be thus. Even when Maitreya appears in the world, it will still be thus.
It is indeed so. Yet, should the Old Man Yama suddenly demand payment for the meals consumed, what then?
But how can one counteract this? Puhua comes out of the Sangha Hall; the Persian enters the bustling marketplace.
On New Year’s Eve: day after day the sun rises in the east; day after day the sun sets in the west. How many cycles of three hundred and sixty days are there?
"Understanding the den. When Xuedou speaks thus, tell me: does this old fellow understand the den?
If you say he understands it, disaster, disaster! If you say he does not understand it, how could he speak in such a way?

If you can be decisive and clear regarding this, you will see that the old year does not depart and the new year does not arrive; one thought-moment is ten thousand years, and ten thousand years are one thought-moment.
Consider this: when Nanshan speaks thus, it is just like a young child following along with red ink. Even an eye-opening monk cannot avoid being laughed at.
But tell me, what excellence does an eye-opening monk possess? He has, of his own accord, a pair of hands that are utterly destitute.
I have never bowed in greeting to ordinary people.
On New Year’s Eve: from ancient times to the present, heaven and earth, the sun and moon, mountains and rivers, and human relations—none of these have shifted by so much as a single hair’s breadth.
If it were merely this, one might think that Lingyin lacks a decisive point; yet we do not realize that it conforms to the world.
It is a reversal: sending off the old and welcoming the new. With a single crack of the firecrackers in the eastern village, the skulls of all people in the great earth are shattered.
Do you wish to recognize the old year? [He] strikes the meditation seat once on the left and says: "Realize it here! Do you wish to recognize the new year?
[He] strikes the meditation seat once on the right and says: "Realize it here! Do you wish to recognize the new year?
The old year is about to pass but has not yet passed; is this where the crisscrossing patterns are joined?
Holding up his staff, he strikes once in the middle and says: "Realize it here! Indeed, if you can place a single eye here, you will not be moved by cold or heat, nor turned by the changing seasons.
Should you still not have realized it, last night the snow accumulated to a depth of three feet.
Snow. In the village ahead, one branch of pine has been broken by the frost.
New Year’s Eve. Heaven has no gate; earth has no door. The golden crow flies, the jade hare runs. Year after year there are three hundred and sixty days;
this year there are three hundred and ninety. The One Qi (Great Pneuma) speaks not; where can one ask the azure heavens? Five years, and again...

[Gate @ Ren]. Even those skilled in calculation cannot exhaust its depths. When pressed to the very night of the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, at the junction where the old year meets the new, from east village to west village, the firecrackers crackle one after another.

Old Man Beichen, taking the non-existent for the existent, cooks a white ox of the open field, burns fire from gnawed-off wood, boils a soup of wild greens, and performs the Village Music. Of all these destitute ghosts, who can equal him? Ling!

I have lived secluded in this courtyard for years, each year being no better than the last. Tonight, pointing at emptiness and tracing through emptiness, I have nothing with which to share the New Year with you all.
Nevertheless, if human sentiment is kind, even drinking water will nourish you. Now tell me, everyone: what do you say?
What is the taste of cold spring water? It is known when the tongue touches it. Heaven and earth cannot compare to it.
On the occasion of the Summer Retreat, a monk asked: "When one takes Great Perfect Enlightenment as one's monastery, what then? He replied: "Look!"
"Clouds atop the tree. The monk said, "Body and mind dwell in peace within the wisdom of equality.

What about that? He replied, "A dreamer’s rambling while fast asleep. The monk said, "Suppose there were a man who, though struck with a great club, would not turn his head back and refuses to enter this monastic community—what then?
He replied, "I have heard the words, but I have not yet seen such a person. The monk said, "Master..."
"Why do you not grasp the meaning? [The student] then prostrated. The Master said, "Who would believe you? He then continued:
"East of the stream, west of the stream—wherever the king provides water and grass, one accepts a little as it comes. North of the mountain, south of the mountain—the ancestral fields and gardens.

When the pure breeze blows vast and wide, at all times throughout the nine months of summer, one dwells in peace everywhere. The mind does not dwell on the profound; the eyes do not hang upon the door. This is what is called..."
This is called "sailing with the wind. Such a person can manage the oars and sails;
yet, when a mad wind sweeps the earth and white waves overturn the sky, one must be a master mariner of iron will to prevail here.
When you hear Jingci speak thus, you may laugh secretly with joy and say, "I understand! I understand! But as for understanding, it is up to you.
I understand. But alas, the wax man from Western Heaven is still unwilling to nod his head. Why? Because there are few guests at the Dragon Gate, while the marketplace is crowded with people.
Again, it is said that a monk asked Nanyuan, "Where have all the patriarchs of the past gone? Nanyuan replied:
"Not ascending to heaven, one enters directly into hell. The monk asked, "What about you, Master? The Abbot said, "Do you know where Baoying has landed?
As the monk hesitated, the Abbot struck him across the mouth with his whisk and called him forward again.
The monk stepped forward. Nan-yuan said, "The order was for you to act," and he struck him once more with his whisk.
Xue-dou said, "Since Nan-yuan’s order was carried out by himself, yet the whisk does not know its own origin—Xue-dou says 'blind'!
This is intended to add frost to snow. Miaoxi said, "To weigh Linji’s Three Mysteries and Three Essentials, one must look to Nan-yuan."
Why is this? Xuedou said, "The whisk does not know its place of origin. Miaoxi also said, "Blind! This was merely an attempt to have both sides meet.
The Master [Zhaozhou] took it up and said: "Although Nanquan’s correct command was fully raised, alas, his life and nature fell into the hands of this monk.
Xuedou and Miaoxi both said 'blind,' yet they could not avoid placing their own bodies in the same spot."
Buried alive. Do you all know where Jingci has landed? A massed cloud stretches across the sea; drawing his sword, he stirs the Dragon Gate.
For the summer retreat: taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery, I wear a cangue upon my head and shackles upon my feet—body and mind [are thus bound].
The summer retreat; the wisdom of equality. Like a weary fish stranded in a dwindling pool, or a sick bird perching on a reed—this is the sphere of activity for the patched-robed monk (*śramaṇa*).
It is like fire melting ice: when one wishes to walk, one walks; when one wishes to sit, one sits. There is no foot to be restrained. Meeting a Buddha, one kills the Buddha;
meeting a Patriarch, one kills the Patriarch. There is no birth to be protected. Yet, turning back to reflect, the Yellow-Faced Gautama did not understand; he met Bodhidharma in delusion. Aha!
What does "scolding" mean? If one is deaf, one loves loud sounds; if one’s eyesight is dim, one requires large characters.
Furthermore, it is recounted that while a monk was standing in attendance upon Baofu, Baofu said, "How can you be so careless? The monk asked, "In what way am I careless?
Baofu took a clod of earth, handed it to the monk, and said, "Throw this outside the gate. The monk then threw it.
[The Master] finished speaking and then asked again, "Where was it that I was careless? Fuku said, "I saw you bumping into things and striking against them;
that is why I said you were careless. The Master commented, "Baofu borrows water to offer flowers.
This monk is lost in broad daylight. Under Nanshan’s gate, everyone is careless, yet they simply dare not speak of it. Why is this?"
Small compassion obstructs great compassion.
Regarding the summer retreat: I observe that the Tathāgata did not come from the past, does not go to the future, and does not abide in the present.

Within this, how could there be room for the two characters "jie-zhi" (the formal commencement of the retreat)? In the kingdom of Magadha, the land is vast and the people are sparse; before the peak of Mount Shaoshi, [it is likewise so].
The wind is high and the moon is cold; only a man of immeasurable capacity can shoulder this burden. Yet, even in the Western Heaven, there are those who would not yet consent to it.

What need is there to speak further of "at all times" or "during the nine months of summer," or of "dwelling in retreat everywhere"? Such is the view of a foul old woman from a village of three households;
do not trouble yourself to bring it forth. The single path above, where the thousand sages have not transmitted it, is as soft as iron and as hard as cotton.
The Layman Lu did not recognize the basic strokes of characters; Chen the Straw-Sandals man carried a board and saw only one side.
"It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing. After noon, the bell for the meal was struck; the Brahmin turned his sandals inside out. When one house has business, a hundred houses are busy.
How could a dragon remain in the den of a shrimp? Suddenly, among the assembly, there may be a monk who recognizes good and ill fortune.
Facing toward the cold ground, he coughed once. Now tell me: how does Nanshan reach a final resolution? He lets out a shout.
"A pickpocket in a noisy place is not yet the true thief. He cites Master Zhunyu:
while the assembly of monks stood in attendance, Zhunyu said, "Just standing here in vain, there is no place for discourse; it is quite stifling. At that time, a monk stepped forward.
[The Master] was about to ask a question when Zhuyou said, "Exerting one's utmost for the sake of the assembly," and then entered the abbot’s quarters.
The Master commented: "Zhuyou’s letting go was majestic; his gathering in was subtle and dense.
As for what he said—'exerting one's utmost for the sake of the assembly'—was it Zhuyou who exerted himself for the assembly, or was it this monk? If anyone can discern this, not only..."
This monk has cleared his grievance; he too walked hand-in-hand with Zhuyou. Had he been unable to discern this, he would have been left in a state of stifled frustration.
Why? Because those who pierce their ears are rarely encountered; most are but men who mark the water's edge.
Entering the summer retreat: before the bell has tolled and the drum has sounded—what a fine model for an ancient Buddha! But when the bell tolls and the drum sounds, everyone comes crowding forward;
in their questions and answers, their suppressions and exaltations, they are seen to be falling apart, seven parts here and eight there.
To the man of clear eyes, there is no fixed pattern: he grasps the nostrils but loses the mouth; he cannot be named and cannot be described. It is right here in Guanyin Temple.

"Maitreya, it is neither the Way nor Chan. A great leviathan swallows the moon as waves surge to the heavens. Stop, stop! His mouth is like the Southern Mountain. During the summer retreat, what serves as proof?
At the two meal times, his strength is coarse from porridge and rice; he takes a stroll by the lake when there is nothing to do.
He cites Dongshan’s night assembly where no lamps were lit; a monk stepped forward to ask a question and then withdrew."
Mount Shàn ordered his attendant to light the lamps. He then called forth the monk who had previously engaged him in dialogue.
As the monk approached, Shàn told him to take some flour—two or three ounces—and give it to this [other] monk. The monk brushed out his sleeves and withdrew; through this, he attained realization.

He subsequently exhausted his clothing and funds to provide a vegetarian feast. Three years later, he came to take leave of Dōngshān. Dōngshān said, "Farewell. At that time, Xuefēng was standing in attendance.
Next, he asked Mount [Shan]: "As for this monk who has just gone away, when will he return?
Shan replied, "He only knows how to go once; he does not know how to come back. The monk returned to his quarters and passed away.
When the news was reported, Shan said, "Even so, he is still three lifetimes behind me. The Master commented: "Dongshan deployed a subtle strategy beforehand; as for this monk..."
Penetrating the heavy barriers in darkness: if you do not attain the subsequent stroke, the previous discourse will be difficult to complete. After a long silence, he said:
"As long as a general possesses a reputation for excellence, even failing to receive a fief is still a barrier."
Winter night. A monk asked: "A monk once asked Yangshan, 'Midwinter is a time of severe cold; this is an annual occurrence. But as for the shifting movement of the sun's course, what is it like?
Yangshan stepped forward, joined his palms, and stood there. What was the meaning of this? The master replied: "He presented a confused and muddled bag of nonsense. The monk asked:
"You knew he could not answer this question, did you not? Wherein lay the intent of Guishan? The master said: "He meant to say that the cold is already upon you."
The Master replied, “There is salt in the sauce. The monk asked, “As for Xiangyan’s saying, ‘I am particularly able to answer this question,’ what does that mean?
The Master replied, “Drawing water and setting fire. The monk asked, “When Yaoshan followed up on the previous statement, why did Xiangyan stand before him with his hands clasped?
The Master replied, “They travel the same road, yet do not share the same tracks. The monk asked, “Yaoshan...”
"Dao asked: 'I rely on meeting Master Jizi, yet he does not understand. Where is it that he does not understand? The answer was: 'The Bodhisattva Dragon King travels, raining down moisture;
his body is shielded by upward-stretching layers of clouds. The monk said: 'It is not that the fathers and sons—Miaoyan, Yangshan, and Daowei—do not follow one another in their singing and clapping.
But tell me, what is the melody? The answer was: 'The Five Indias cannot blow it up; it is the Han land.'"
Hewanqi said, “I thank the Master for his reply,” and then prostrated. The Master then said: “The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence;
the gateless is the Dharma-gate. As for this gateless gate, one must find its opening and enter.
Have any of you ever managed to enter? [He] took up his staff, struck it once, and said: ‘Enter from here! If you can enter, then do as you please.’”
In the four directions and eight corners, if you have not yet attained entry, this mountain monk cannot help but suppress his majestic light to sketch a shadow for you all:
To the south of Zhaozhou is the Stone Bridge; within the Guanyin Monastery is Maitreya.
The Patriarch left behind a single sandal, which even to this day cannot be found. Western India’s Sanskrit, here in this land rendered in the Tang language: the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Regarding the Piṭaka of Treatises (*śāstrapiṭaka*): is there still this news? When the ancients spoke in such a manner, what was their intent?
Even if one were to hear this and nod in secret, one would still not escape being dead beneath the words.

You must know that from the mountains and rivers of past and present, to the heavens and earth of past and present, to human relations of past and present, and to the sun and moon of past and present—not even a hair’s breadth has shifted. All matters since the beginningless kalpas are [thus].
"At this very moment—how is it with the matter of this very moment? After a long silence, he said: "The first line of the hexagram Jiujiu (Nine Nines) has emerged, signifying the birth of Yang.

He then related an anecdote: A monk came to visit Master Zhaozhou at his assembly. They were competing for the position of First Seat (*di-yi zuo*), and the administrative official reported this to Zhaozhou.
Zhaozhou said, "Let them all be made Second Seats. The official asked, "Who then shall be made the First Seat? Zhaozhou replied, "The one who is dressed [in the robes]."

[The Master] was applying incense. Having finished preparing the incense for the ritual, he informed the Prefect. The Prefect said, "The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, the fragrance of wisdom, and the fragrance of liberation.

The Master remarked: "Old Zhao’s response to the occasion was like the wind blowing across water. As for the First Seat saying, 'Incense smoke has arisen,' it is as if one were dreaming of the stench of sweat in a donkey-year."

The winter solstice: days grow bright while nights grow dark; the sun departs and the moon arrives. Thus it is that the One Qi (Great Purity) acts spontaneously without being so, and the myriad transformations arise without being made.
If you go forth in this very manner, there are countless dead people upon level ground. Yet for the functioning of a patch-robed monk, there are its own established rules:
the Dipper turns and the stars shift; the east surges up and the west sinks down. Have you not seen how Muzhou asked Yangshan during the severity of mid-winter?

"A cold year, year after year. As for the matter of the shifting movement of the sun's shadow, what is it like? Yangshan stepped forward and stood with his hands joined at his chest; his feet were as black as lacquer.
Guishan said, "I knew from the start that you could not answer this question. (This is like) "A father conceals his son’s faults.
Xiangyan said, "I am particularly able to answer this question. (This is like) "When a family is wealthy, the children are spoiled. Guishan then asked, "The severe mid-winter..."

"The matter of the cold year after year. As for the shifting of the sun's course, what is it like? Xiangyan also stepped forward, stood with hands clasped, and indeed possessed another depth of realization.
Guishan said, "Fortunately, Jizi does not understand; the more one tries to hide it, the more it is revealed.
Such was Guishan’s way of holding up the matter, such were the two disciples' responses, and such was Shitian’s pointing and commentary. Does this truly suffice?
"Is this a matter within the *zongcheng* (the vehicle of the lineage)? After a long silence, he said: "From of old, no one has recognized the merit of sweating horses in battle;
it is only necessary to re-discuss the epoch-making achievement. He then cited the case of Chief Seat Dingshan. Once, while Dingshan was washing his robes, he asked, "What are you doing?

The chief seat held up the robe. Dingshan said, "What kind of robe is that which you are washing? The chief seat replied, "In Fuzhou, they use iron coins. Dingshan then called for the *weina* (the disciplinarian).
He moved down to take up residence. The Master commented: "Dingshan may be said to have 'borrowed a hand to perform a fist-fight'; his spirit and bearing were immediate.
Although the Head Seat lost his money and suffered for it, his elegance endures for a thousand ages. Had it been Shitian, when Dingshan asked, 'What is that which is being washed?
he would have cupped water in his hands and splashed it out—this would have been a thousand times better than Dingshan."
Mountains—how could one avoid being reduced to a state of utter embarrassment?
On the Winter Solstice, Śākyamuni spoke what was not spoken; Kāśyapa heard what was not heard. A sharp sword cuts through empty space, and the ten thousand phenomena resound with a "pao-pao.
To proceed in this manner is to inherit echoes and grasp at shadows; such instances are as numerous as dust motes and sands. The family of Xie is not at home; they are out fishing.
A boat. Mistaking orange peel for fire, they say: "The depths of the School of the Patriarchs are profound;

when measured against one's own mind, coarse food satisfies easily, but chewing finely leaves one hungry. If you are a man of superior spirit, turn over your iron face, raise your Amoghasiddhi eyes, and leap from the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff—only then will you not shatter.
Beyond Mount Sumeru, beckoning with a hand, he cannot be called back.

Return. To casually take up a single pivot and reveal a single realm is entirely within the state prior to the existence of either sentient beings or Buddhas—a place where the sun and moon do not reach.

Nevertheless, even so, there is still someone within Biepan Rock who refuses to nod their head. Why? Because the Zhao jade was originally without flaw;
it was Xiangru who deceived the King of Qin. Again, he cites the kōan of Dongshan inviting Head Seat Tai to eat fruit.
The Master comments: "This case has been around for a long time. Everyone says that the Head Seat’s words were not [in accord with]..."

On the eve of the year, the golden crow hastens and the jade hare speeds; light follows darkness, and darkness follows light, revolving without ceasing.
Tonight, success has been achieved. At the break of dawn, with a single cry from the golden cock, the old year passes into the new.
Neighbors to the east and west—the Old Li and Brother Zhang—vie with one another to offer congratulations. Even the monks’ alms bowls have turned their heads to look on.
Wet twice a day, drifting along effortlessly; unaware of whether the month is large or small, regardless of the intercalary days of the year.
Gazing at the azure heavens, one simply passes the time in this manner. Yet when tested and scrutinized, it may seem similar, but it is not yet truly so.
Therefore, Master Yunfeng Yue addressed the assembly during a year-end *xiaocan*, saying: "You lot, this group of later..."
"Born! You certainly do not know the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Śāstras. You enter the assembly to practice Zen, yet you do not understand Zen.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, how will you settle the account? When you hear Yunfeng speak thus, does it not make your face burn with shame and cause your sweat to pour?
How can you escape from Yunfeng’s circle? Although Shitian is incapable, he dares to beg for the help of Muduo.
"Venerable Elder, let us provide these people with a moment of sudden liberation. He suddenly picked up his staff, struck the ground once, and said:

"Where the land of Wu ends at the river, beyond the bank are many mountains of Yue. He then cited Deshan’s address to the assembly: "Tonight there is a small-scale retreat; I will not answer questions.

[The monk] had not yet asked why he was being struck. Deshan said, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "I am a man from Silla.
Deshan said, "Before you have even stepped onto the ship's railing, you deserve thirty blows. The Master [Linji] commented:
"This old fellow Deshan first terrified people to death and later made them laugh to death. If this monk had not entered the tiger’s den, how could he have seized the tiger’s cub? Now...
An informal evening discourse: If there is a question, I shall answer; if there is no question, I shall simply rest. Furthermore, I am unable to bring myself to strike with the staff. Why?
Because the nine provinces and four seas are as clear as a mirror; one may walk along the official path or through the hall at one's own ease.
The Year’s Night: Buddhist Dharma and worldly dharma; worldly dharma and Buddhist Dharma—these are one, yet have many aspects; they are two, yet are not of two kinds.
Like hooks and locks, interlocking rings, or a blade that cannot be pried open, the tattered and patched robes of the patch-robed monk encompass heaven and earth.
With his staff, he carries the sun and moon upon his head; at his waist, he possesses a calendar of many years that does not shift with the seasonal changes of the four times.
Shifting from here to there, penetrating to the very top and to the very bottom—these words are called "grasping the brush and following the vermilion ink," which everyone knows.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, a rat enters a cow's horn. What is the single path for leaving the body?
