The Master commented: "Zhaozhou exerted too much effort; this monk did not listen to the matter truly. If one were to ask, 'Regarding Nanshan, what is the meaning of non-transmigration?'"
"Meaning. He struck with his staff in a harmonious tone. "Why? Because Mount Nan-shan has never deceived or misled a teacher-monk.

On the night of the year’s end, the creation of heaven and earth involves both the hidden and the manifest. The sun, moon, and stars have their brightness and their obscurity; rain, dew, wind, and frost involve both life and death;
the succession of the four seasons involves both the new and the old—all of these are matters of duality. The patched-robed monk..."
In the monastic community, upon this ball of red flesh, there stands a precipice ten thousand fathoms high. Day after day throughout the twelve periods, it remains ever the same;
year after year throughout the twelve months, it is always one and the same. Moving spontaneously and freely, freely and spontaneously—whether eyes are closed or open.
Today is the New Year. From the beginning, one’s nostrils have reached the heavens; who cares about many years and dates?
Even so, as the year ends and the age concludes, there is the "knots and crisscrosses" of the turning-body phrase. How would you say it? After a long silence, he said:
"The sky is clear, yet one knows not where the clouds have gone; the earth is cold, preserving the snow for a long time. He then cited Xuansha asking Changsheng:
"I observe the Tathāgata: he does not come from the past, he does not go to the future, and he does not abide in the present.
Elder, what do you say? Sheng said, "Grant me passage; there is a place to speak. Sha said, "I grant you passage.
What do you say? Sheng remained silent. Sha said, "Who will understand? Sheng said, "The Master does not understand. Sha said, "I knew it all along."
"You are making your living inside a ghost cave. The Master picked up [the subject] and said: "Changsheng lives inside a ghost cave;
has Xuansha escaped it yet? If Linji’s command were in effect, his skull would have been smashed to pieces."
On the eve of the New Year: How high is heaven? How thick is the earth? To the south, north, east, and west, the crow flies and the hare runs. Light turns to darkness, and darkness turns to light.

On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, we collectively call this the "end of the year" and the "exhaustion of the age. But tell me, does the year and its seasons have a time of ultimate exhaustion?
If there were a point of exhaustion, there would necessarily be a point of origination. So tell me, from what does it begin?
From where does it arise? If you attempt to grasp the void by twisting and wringing it with your own intellect, you will inevitably labor your spirit in vain.
Little do you realize that the seventy-two seasonal signs and twenty-four solar energies reside right upon the tips of your noses. At such a moment, how can one utter a word of joining the palms?
After a long silence, he said: "The new year’s horn has already blown atop the city walls; yet before the window, the incense still flickers."
The Lantern of the Old Year. Again, he cited the case where a monk arrived at He-lin and knocked on the door. He-lin asked, "Who is it? The monk said, "A wandering monk.
He-lin said, "Do not say 'wandering monk. Even if the Buddha came, he would not be admitted.
The monk asked, "Why would he not be admitted? He-lin said, "There is no place for you to lodge. The Master commented: "How great was He-lin! He brought this defeat upon himself."—Nan-shan.
I have a point of view that I wish for everyone to know together. Now that you know it, why do you not put it into practice even when encountering a Buddha?
It is easy to get along when meeting others, but difficult to live together with them as human beings.
The Summer Retreat Ends. In the past, Mañjuśrī spent the summer retreats in three places; this summer at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he observes the *anagārika* (rainy-season retreat) in a single location.
With "nails for a beak and iron tongues," when a patch-robed monk arrives here, take it for granted that he will be unable to offer an explanation.

Since he cannot offer an explanation, how can he avoid "closing his eyes and eating a snail"—a truly bitter and acrid ordeal? At Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, there is a method for finding a place to settle atop a tree. Now...
At night, I intended to entrust this to everyone. Enough, enough! When one knows how to practice medicine, illness is rare;
when one knows the measure of life, there is little sorrow. [The Master] raised the case where Yunmen asked a monk: "In the early autumn, at the end of summer, you brothers go east and west.

Suppose someone suddenly asks you on the way ahead: 'How will you respond? What would you say? The monk said, "The assembly has already withdrawn. Yunmen said, "Give me back my ninety days' worth of rice!"

"Money! Money! The Master offered this verse: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, tens of thousands upon tens of thousands; The path of Stonehead is slippery, and the soles of one's feet are worn through.
This monk turns his body swiftly upon the edge of a sword, Yet he too must pay the rice-money to Yunmen."
The Elder Fayu Fu appeared in the world and requested instructions before the Duizi Stupa;
he was entrusted with the *saṃghāṭī* robe, which has remained until the present day without its lineage being severed. He is what is called the "Foremost Ancestor."
This is not understood. The calamity will extend to one's descendants. Having entered the Buddha’s gate and partaken of the Buddha’s food, this vast and magnificent lineage requires support;
yet such support must come from a man of true caliber. Moreover, you call yourself an Elder (*sthavira*). Since your title is such, how should your reality correspond?

Possessing eyes that look upward, one attains great capacity and great function; thus one may open and cultivate those among humans and devas, benefiting later students, and will not fail the two characters for "transcending the world.
Speaking specifically of those with middling or inferior capacities, they too must recognize cause and effect and maintain their ritual observances (*kōmō*).

Morning and evening, they should never slacken in meditation and recitation. Whether establishing new works or repairing old ones, in all circumstances, they should employ a mind and body of true reality.

Only then will there be a slight degree of correspondence. One cannot sit in the abbot’s quarters and expect realization to be manifest. Those who are diligent place the blame on others; those who are indolent claim credit for themselves.
In the space of a mere instant, the head turns white and the teeth turn yellow. There is much more to come ahead. This is the way of the former generations and the elder masters.
When the time and conditions have arrived, there is nothing that can be done. To "tear open the skin of the face" mostly occurs after one has entered a monastery;

yet, regardless of whether the monastery is large or small, or whether the assembly is numerous or few—whether amidst a crowd of thousands or tens of thousands, or in a place where one stays alone—the same applies.
Throughout the two and six periods of the day and night, one should single-mindedly keep this Way in mind.
Through long-term, uninterrupted effort, one is thus able to bring forth realization. Elder Fú, we have been together at Nanshan for several years.

Since you have gone out into the world at Ningguo, although the monastery is of the "ten directions" (public) type, everything ultimately depends on the person. Before Mazu and Baizhang, there was no position of abbot;
yet even then, it was necessary to have a place of ten directions before it could not be called a *conglin* (monastic community). If...
To make such distinctions is to abandon the root and pursue the branches; it is not worth mentioning. An ancient said, "If you only obtain the root, do not worry about the branches.
The exchange of staffs and shouts is the branch; the words and phrases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are the branch. Ultimately, what is the root?
"Obtaining the seat and donning the robe"—look for yourself after this.
To the Zen practitioner Shijue:
In the eye, not even a grain of sand can enter; in the ear, not even a drop of water can enter. Why is this? If there were even a single thread of thought, it would remain a single thread of thought.
[In such a state,] a Mount Sumeru could enter the eye, and the four great oceans could enter the ear. If there were...
"A single strand of hair—it is not a single strand of hair. Only after passing through these two gates can one truly enter the practice.
Generally speaking, those who study the Way must also pry open the eye at the crown of their heads and distinguish between the muddy water and the pure silk;
only then are they fit for entry. There are some fellows who always rely on arbitrary fabrication and patchwork, remaining muddled and vague, treating it all as a single phrase.
He said, "One is all; all is one. Entering a desolate field, one does not discriminate; one simply picks up whatever grass comes to hand.

This may seem similar, yet it is not so. To reach this point—to stand alone with feet planted on the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, or to have a bronze alms bowl filled to the brim with oil—one must be a true man indeed.
Juechan remained for a long time; as he was about to depart...
Seeking words, one is unconsciously distracted; unaware of this, one does not know whether one has returned to understanding or is merely nodding in confusion.
Should this still be the case, it matters whether the eyes are open or closed.

This "Shiguanshu" (Record of Observations) sets forth the teachings of the two schools of Confucianism and Buddhism. Each values its own gate. Since we have already discarded our former forms, shaved our hair, and donned the cassock, we naturally have matters pertaining to that cassock.
If, while practicing the Way, one has surplus energy, one may peripherally search the Confucian classics to gain a rough understanding of them.
A general outline may suffice. Yet, people often become mired in details without knowing how to return to the source; they inevitably chase after the finger while losing sight of the moon.
If one must exhaustively seek its ultimate limit, why not simply reach the ultimate limit of our own tradition?

Even if one possesses the talent for carving and engraving, or excels in literature throughout the world, it is a pity that since antiquity, such scholars have all served as mere clerks to me—what do they have to do with me? The ancients still...

It means merely writing down one's name at the foot of the document; how much more so for a person like me, who stands outside the conventional world? Observing that you have gathered here for a long time, your natural disposition is fond of learning;
even in the depths of winter or the height of summer, your books do not leave your hands. When these expressions are manifested in your speech, they are compared to those of previous years.
When he first came to Nanshan, I perceived that he was making significant progress. I advised him, saying, "Let this level of literary composition suffice; what need is there for further effort?
If you apply yourself here with firm resolve and diligent strength, you will suddenly pull out the nostrils [of the Buddha-nature].
This is no mere metaphor. Although he responded with respectful agreement before me, I did not yet know whether he truly accepted this in his heart. One day—
Upon parting, I went to Mount Zhongshan to see Chijue, who requested a verse on paper. Having no means to satisfy his request, I recalled a verse by an ancient master which says:
"The pillar before the courtyard has long been pregnant; It has given birth to a son, truly most handsome.
Before he understands speech, he composes a rhapsody; With one stroke, he shall take the top honors. What was the intent behind these words?
This is not for the sake of providing answers to examination questions for students of the present day, such as those who achieved the rank of *zhuangyuan* through the compositions of Chao and Dong.

Rather, it is for my own family’s "passing the examination with an empty mind"—the foremost kind of *zhuangyuan*. Those who act with purposeful effort should also be like this; observe and test it for yourself, and you will know that my words are not false.
Consequently, I have composed twenty-eight characters and send them along with this letter. As for that matter of my family, there is truly nothing [to boast of].
Abundant! It does not reside in the frequent rummaging of old papers. Before understanding a single word, one first composes a rhapsody;
then one visits Mount Zhong to ask, "How is it?"—this was shown to Attendant Shao Wen.
The depths of the Chan school require one to gauge its essence within one’s own breast. A coarse meal may easily satisfy hunger, but chewing delicately will not prevent one from starving.
That the fundamental is not clear stems entirely from one’s own errors. In the study of Zen there is no other way: one must first clarify the fundamental before success can be attained.

If you instead pluck leaves and seek branches, you will err until the time of Maitreya’s appearance in the world; you will ultimately never strike the mark. Remember the National Teacher’s three calls.
The Attendant. There were three responses from the attendant. The National Teacher said, "I thought it was I who owed you;
it turns out it is you who owe me. Now tell me, where does the meaning of his three calls lie? You must look at the very root before you can understand.
Regarding this koan, the various quarters have produced countless commentaries, each based on their own contemporary perspective; some of them possess five or six parts of the truth.
"Or perhaps seven or eight parts are similar. Old Zhaozhou adds a footnote, saying: "It is like a person writing characters in the air;

though the characters themselves do not take shape, the traces of their colors are already manifest. Zhaozhou has captured it to the extent of nine parts and nine-tenths of a centimeter, yet there remains one-tenth of a centimeter of ambiguity.
When Wen came to Nanshan to join the assembly, I asked him to stay in the attendant’s quarters for one year. I, the old monk, followed [him]...
I see him face-to-face and speak the Dharma; how could it be limited to three calls? He also responds according to his capacity;
how could it be limited to three responses? Tell me, is there any principle of the Buddha-Dharma here or not? If you can understand this, you will know the subtle point of Zhaozhou’s "one hair.
If you do not understand, you must strictly avoid the fabrication of arbitrary interpretations. Only when your eyes open in the future will you realize the old monk’s intent.
Nor do they fail one another.

To show that he has attained the ancestral gate and the vast livelihood of the abbot of Shengjian Monastery, he requires a person of great strength and capacity who alone is fit to bear this responsibility.

If one possesses small faculties and little wisdom, there is still a chance for them to gain understanding. Have you not seen how Yantou saw Deshan and immediately asked, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage?
Deshan then gave a shout, and Yantou immediately prostrated himself. This is like gold being weighed against gold or water being poured into water—what seams or gaps could there be to seek out?
Dongshan said, "If it were not for Master Huo, it would have been very difficult to take on. This is praise indeed.
"Attained. Yantou said, "Old man Dongshan, what do you know of good and evil?
You have no idea that at that time I was holding up with one hand and pressing down with the other. Yantou was stripped of his heart, liver, and five viscera by Dongshan’s single phrase;
possessing the eye of a student, he was able to see through it. Is there anyone such a master nowadays? Truly, they are like picking out stars from the night sky."

Yue Sheng traveled extensively, visiting various regions and remaining in assembly for many years. Suddenly, he conceived the desire to seek the Way elsewhere and came specifically to the abbot’s quarters to request a verse from me.
I wrote with rapid brushstrokes, speaking profusely; yet opening one's mouth is not merely a matter of the tongue.
If Yue Sheng had a pearl in his eye, he would never have fished for it beneath my words.
They point to the Elder bowing and the Flower being plucked with a smile; it is like a burning brick striking the frozen ground to its very core. They speak of severing the arm to find peace of mind;

it is like Red-Eye bumping into a firebrand. From this point on, they have sought one another through successive generations, receiving the empty and connecting the echoes, and thus they say: "To erect the Dharma-banner and establish the fundamental tenet."
Throughout all directions, the world is vast and expansive; boundaries are demarcated and territories divided, each asserting its own hegemony.

From the time it was cooked and divided among five houses, it has been manipulated and played with until this very day. Only the single lineage of Linji remains unbroken, yet even this life hangs by a thread.

The Buddha-dharma is not like this. There is no one to advocate for it, and no one to lift it up; inevitably, it suffers from the maladies of being "like a knife and a blade" or the confusion between "fish and ru.
Why does it suffer from these maladies? Because in later generations, monasteries have abandoned the root and pursued the branches, speaking of them at great length.
It is not that there is a lack of practice; rather, when it comes to profound discourse on the principles, there is certainly no deficiency.
If one were to verify this in the future, it would be more than just half a month's journey ahead of those ancients. As the old Dongshan said: "In other quarters they speak of Chan;
here we practice Chan. This is precisely what he meant. For ten years I have been at Nanshan, and it was exactly during this time that monks came and went in great numbers.
In this place, I have never seen a single person who has not entered the gate of the Buddha-dharma.
Brothers, you present me with long songs and short verses that fill volumes whenever you move; yet where, ultimately, does the fundamental matter lie?
Li arrived here from Chaoyang to spend the summer retreat, his resolve firm and certain. Upon first arriving at Nanshan, he brought incense and inquired about how to apply himself to practice. I—
I could not help but show him the matter of his own fundamental nature. At the end of the summer, he came again to the abbot’s quarters and requested another saying to serve as a self-admonition.
I said, "Elder, did you not hear the old monk speak throughout this entire summer? He smiled and said:
"Alas, how difficult it is to fill a pit to its depths! I said to him: "If you wish to fill the pit, bury me, an old monk, right inside it!
Is there anyone who can bring themselves to do so? Before the spade has even moved, one is already within it.
It would be better for Mañjuśrī to remain Mañjuśrī and liberation to remain liberation; let each person put on their own robes and eat their own food, so as to avoid mutual entanglement."

To instruct the Chan practitioner Long, [the Master] wished to transform a live snake into a living dragon. First, he poured poison down its throat, allowing it to feel the prickling of needles filling its belly;
then he cast it into the vast and boundless surging waves. This verse was composed by a great elder of former generations to manifest the essence of the Zen school.
The Master spoke these words: "Grasp the meaning of the hook; do not fixate on the zero point of the scale.

If you are like those who merely parrot the words, poring over them with intellectual calculations—'What is it like? 'How is it?'—then even the ancients could not have bent you. Where would you find relief?
It requires such a person to clarify such a matter. Therefore it is said: 'When it is attained in the mind, *eranda* becomes sandalwood.'"
To lose the essence of this tree is to turn the nectar of immortality into a garden of thorns. In the mere space between turning one’s hand over and back, benefit and harm become utterly distinct.
To gallop upon the edge of an icicle or to lay one’s body across the blade of a sword—there is another path for the Chan practitioner to turn about, like cutting through nails and severing iron.
To the monks of the Five Lakes and the practitioners with their single staffs who have not yet seen Shitō: you may harbor doubts, but once you have seen him,
you will realize he is simply an old monk with white hair and yellowed teeth, his features rugged and weathered— a mere old priest of Zen and the Buddha-way.
The Dharma. Where does it reside? Here, within the eye, there is a pearl. It is certain that one obtains fire and smoke by begging for them;
one carries the spring and wears the moon back home. If you are slow and hesitant, you will turn toward the pigments beneath the mind. A single vajra arrow.
"Passing through the crown of the head—where does one go? For this reason, when Chan Master Chen Muzhou called to a monk, the monk turned his head;
Muzhou said, "A fellow carrying a wooden board. He further said, "This is a settled case; I grant you thirty blows.
This old ghost has placed a load of one hundred and twenty catties upon people's shoulders, desiring only that they lift it and go forth immediately. How could this be...?
Guests follow one after another; if you wish to grasp the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, there is no such "meaning" from the West for you to investigate.
You must sever the red thread beneath your feet to become a man of the Way who is free from concerns.

If that red thread is not severed, it will entangle you in hundreds of layers and thousands of folds, like an iron net stretching across the void—how could you ever penetrate it? Even if you were to penetrate it, what lies ahead...

There is a great matter here. Those who have not undergone bitter toil do not know it. Only when you have penetrated it will you realize that Shitian was not one who struck terror into people at a moment of crisis.
*Dot!* Have you even mastered his somnolent talk?
To show this to the Chan practitioner Zhuzhong:
when Gautama held up the flower and Kāśyapa smiled, it was decisively beyond the five thousand and forty-eight fascicles [of the scriptures].
It is like playing a lute made of a lion’s sinew—when it is struck, all other sounds are silenced. Scholars of the present day, for the most part, do not recognize the vital lineage; they merely...
Divining in vain, following the current until one is drenched; there is no knowing where it will end—this is truly pitiable.

One who understands the timing and distinguishes between fortune and misfortune will, even from three thousand *li* away, see the wind and cast down their weapons. Yet, this is still a matter of minor calculation.

Should they step forward, they cannot avoid ultimately returning to the sea of death. Do not say the house is not established; the son who establishes the house has not yet been born. Do not say the house...
It will not be destroyed. The sons who have broken the household are not yet grown; only those born later who possess resolve can bear this heavy burden of the Buddha-dharma.
If it were otherwise, one need not fear that the Buddha-dharma would rot away.

The Elder Jue appeared in the world seeking words from those above—whether Buddhas or patriarchs—and found that they had no dharma to give others; they merely revealed a small portion of what is right before one's eyes.

Only those who possess spiritual bone from past lives can know its point of rest upon a single utterance. When one investigates its ultimate aim, it is a medicine for those who are already free of illness. Therefore, [it is] "clamped" (jia).
When Shanjian saw Chuanzzi, he was struck twice with the oars; Chuanzzi nodded his head three times.

When Fachang encountered Quandao and requested instruction, Quandao simply took off his robe, shook it out, and showed it to him. One must know that this matter does not reside in words; there is no pointing and no transmission.
Only when one personally arrives at it oneself will the mind find rest and the will cease. Once one is able to find such rest, [the matter is settled].

Binding the waist with three strands of rattan, dwelling on mountains wherever one may be—whether in thatched huts or stone chambers—without discrimination, one lets go completely for ten or twenty years, as if in a state of stupor or intoxication.
When the fruit ripens and the Way becomes fragrant, there will naturally be fellow practitioners who, brushing aside the grass and gazing at the wind, come from afar to seek instruction.
Suddenly, having caught one or two of them, they take them as seeds for the future, causing them to...
The succession remains uninterrupted. Together we repay the profound kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, so that neither may fail the original vow of renunciation.

Having resided among the assembly for many years, Lingfeng’s seat remained vacant. The Provincial Governor sent representatives from the various mountains to recommend candidates, and I was included among those nominated.
The Prefecture dispatched an official to deliver a formal notice (gōtō). Jaku refused to come out.

I exhorted him by citing the words of the ancients regarding their indifference toward thatched huts or stone chambers. Reluctantly, Jaku complied with the command. He asked for a verse to serve as a warning, which I provided, saying:
"The ancients called this 'the lion teaching its cub' or 'the secret of deluding the child. Why need one be so tedious? From head to tail."
Half-closed and half-open; apply yourself directly and proceed. You have not yet escaped being scrutinized by Old Man Wang of the Eastern Village.
Go, exert yourself!
To the practitioner of Chan who has returned to his hometown, I beg for words.
In the lineage of the Patriarchs, wild weeds reach to the heavens; should one wish to seek and contemplate them, white clouds stretch ten thousand miles.
Thus, when Deshan beckoned with his hand, Gaoting strode straight across. To enter this gate, one must raise one and clarify the three.

Discerning the slightest detail with the precision of a scale’s beam and weight, one still fears the arrow will pass beyond Silla; how much more so when seeking it from the mold of the ancients or at the lips of the Master?
To labor the mind and spirit in such a way is to remain a dreamer even for the year of a donkey’s birth.

You practitioners of Zen have gathered here for four years; as you depart, you requested words of advice, so I have written this to leave behind. Return to the three-family village, to the crossroads.
"Head! It strikes the author. But if you can bring it up in this way, and suddenly there is one or half a person who nods their head sideways—that is the moment when the old monk’s words circulate."
To show the Great Way of the Chan master Quan:
it is utterly beyond comparison; each goes their own way, east or west. Like a spark from a flint, nothing can catch up; like a flash of lightning, nothing can penetrate.
This is merely the ancient masters speaking of setting up models and drawing patterns. Have you all ever scrutinized and chewed upon this? To blink your eyebrows is already to miss it.
It is already past. How much more so for one who has become a eunuch with trimmed whiskers? One would likely find there is no connection whatsoever.
Only when you can turn your body and breathe freely within that place where there is no connection will you finally know: "Where the level marshes end is the green mountain;
the traveler stands even beyond the green mountain. Having come to Cold Spring to gather together, I suddenly felt homesickness and requested words upon a sheet of paper from my sleeve.

I say this to you: in recent years, the fires of war have raged across Western Sichuan. How could one advance under such conditions? Here, disregarding all peril and ruin, one must take that single step forward.
Amidst ten thousand deaths, one recovers one’s wretched life; thus, one comes to realize the meaning of “visiting one’s own home” and meeting with Ciming.
In years past, amidst the chaos of war, I went to study under Fenyang; for the sake of the Dharma and for the sake of my parents, there was no distinction between the two.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when the four mountains close in? Zhaozhou said, "I, the old monk, am also within them.
The monk said, "Is there still a way to seek escape? Zhaozhou said, "If you are already therein, then you seek escape from therein. Here, not even a speck of dust is moved.
Only by capturing the old man of Zhaozhou can one truly establish my school’s lineage.
To show the great cause and condition of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to the Zen practitioner Xing, it is certainly not something that those of minor capacity can bear; one must take it up...
Formerly, one must at once cast down all evil cognitions and evil thoughts; only then can one find the path of death here.
Once the path of death is found, one must further seek the path of life; only then will there be a slight degree of resonance.

Should one, however, be shadowy and echo-like, hesitant and doubtful, one cannot avoid losing one's way in the midst of the day. Therefore it is said: "The treading of dragons and elephants is not that of donkeys."
That which can be endured. Does the king of geese who selects the milk not differ from the class of ducks? Is it not so? Alas! Few are the guests at the Dragon Gate;
many are the people in the bustling marketplace.

To Zen practitioner Shiri, at the end of summer and the beginning of autumn: among the monastics, some are returning to their native lands while others are traveling to other regions. Occasionally, there are those who seek words upon paper.
I say to them: "This matter does not reside within words. Is not the entire Great Canon of Gautama [the Buddha] sufficient?"
Is this mere words? Why then did the Old Barbarian come from the West, transmitting a separate tradition outside the teachings?
Thus, when Luzu saw a monk approaching, he simply faced the wall; when Magu saw Liangsu coming, he took his hoe and went straight into the garden.
Even the various great masters—some striking the ground with their staffs, some holding up pitchforks, some beating drums, or some rolling balls—all of these were direct.
Severing and upholding: there is only a mere fragment revealed before one's eyes. One must have a nature of sharp and keen faculties;
with a single glance, one penetrates through. What else is there to do? If you seek Zen or seek the Way from the mouths of others, on the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month—
You have wasted this skin-sack; what regret could possibly avail? Zen practitioner Ni, you have long resided at Reizan (Cold Spring).
Now, having suddenly come to bid me farewell and seeking words of instruction, I have written these tangled vines to briefly satisfy your request.

If you were a man of true caliber, you would have leaped out from this very thicket of weeds and soared into the Milky Way, thereby manifesting the original nature of a true practitioner of the Way. Should you hesitate even further, the arrow will have already passed.
Xi Qin. How far-reaching it is! [The Master] reveals to Chan Master Xian of Nan-kang that the Way resides within the ordinary activities of daily life;
it does not involve discursive thought, nor does it fall within the range of speech. To give rise to a single thought or stir a single intention—[is already to stray]. White.

Clouds stretch ten thousand miles. When the Old Barbarian came from the West, he originally had no separate dharma to give to people; he simply said: "Directly pointing to the human mind, seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha.
The mind is the mind one inherently possesses; the Buddha is the Buddha of one's own true nature. What business has it with others?
Therefore, when the Second Patriarch requested the pacification of his mind, the Old Barbarian said: "Bring forth your mind, and I will pacify it for you."
The Patriarch said, "When you seek the mind, it is utterly unattainable. The Old Barbarian said, "I have finished settling your mind for you.
This is precisely like offering flowers with water; how could one ever add even a single drop of external seasoning?
All other ancient worthies were likewise direct manifestations, intending for people to grasp the meaning directly right here. Seeing that you did not understand, he drew out this model.
It is like polishing a brick to make a mirror, or striking a cart and striking an ox—is this not a model? It is like throwing a sword into the air;
whether it reaches its mark or not is irrelevant, for the void leaves no trace and the blade suffers no loss—is this not a model?
It is like the earth supporting a mountain, yet the earth does not know the mountain’s solitary loftiness; it is like a stone containing jade, yet the stone does not know the jade’s purity.
Xia. If one can be thus, this is true renunciation; is this not a model?

Even when taking up a single pivot to reveal a single realm—looking toward the southeast while the mind’s intent lies in the northwest—the clever man, from three thousand miles away, is like water poured into water.
It is only the dull-witted master who mistakenly takes brown sugar for honey. Upon whom does the fault lie? First...
This is the senior brother of Master Guyuan; they are teacher and disciple from the two mountains, North and South.

When this mountain monk meets them, he merely offers a greeting of *he-nan* (bowing with palms joined). I have never provided them with any formal model, nor was it ever my practice to stand behind people with hands clasped.
You should strive to follow this diligently.
To show the Chan practitioner Ren:
what is it that a man of high standing on pilgrimage (*xingjiao*) ought to do? It is not merely to wear tight, sturdy straw sandals and travel about in all directions;
that is called "pilgrimage. One must encounter a true and authentic master to investigate that one fundamental matter prior to the birth of one's parents.
Make the head straight and the tail straight; bring it forth, penetrating from top to bottom.

On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, at the brink of life and death, when you must let go of your hands and feet—if you can truly apply it then, only then will you not have brought shame upon yourself. Yet now, you run hither and thither.
