Distinguish between the great and the small. Regarding gain and sustenance, do not calculate their thickness or thinness; regarding suffering and joy, or adversity and favor, there is no difference between them.
If one can truly practice these two lines, the affairs of a lifetime are settled. As the Fifth Patriarch said: "While others everywhere preach Chan, here we practice Chan.
This naturally accords with the hidden truth: the lanterns and the pillars are all fellow practitioners; the mountains, rivers, and the vast earth are fundamentally nothing other than this.
There is. Furthermore, there is one more phrase; the old monk’s mouth is too narrow to explain it through for you.
You shall obtain the sitting robe and look into it yourself hereafter.
A Dharma Talk by Meng Jie-xiang, Minister of Works (Hui), upon the Arrival of a Portrait of His Eminence at Bao Temple on the Fifth Day of the Twelfth Month.
On the fifth day of the twelfth month, there was a man of immense capacity who came from the West.

Suddenly appearing before this mountain monk, he exchanged greetings and conversation in a manner entirely ordinary. Fortunately, all was well; yet, for no apparent reason, he suddenly claimed to have captured the "Numinous."
The Great Master presented the true evidence to this mountain monk for inspection. This mountain monk examined it closely and saw that it was merely unclaimed property.

There is no need to trouble yourself with further investigation of such evidence. Finally, the Master again commanded this mountain monk to provide a turning phrase; yet, there is no place where one may speak.
"There is nowhere where it cannot be spoken. This gives rise to excessive weariness.

Little do you realize that every day this mountain monk puts on his straw sandals and passes through the belly of the Non-Monastery hundreds of times. Since you are an insider of the house, how could you remain unaware?
Now tell me: where shall we settle this man of immeasurable capacity who came before? We shall send him to Bao-shou’s Guest House and hang him high up there.
We shall burn incense to fume his nostrils and have every monk from the five lakes and four seas come to examine him one by one.
Let us see how thick this fellow’s skin is! *Duḥ!* (A shout)
A Dharma Talk for the Zen Practitioner Cheng:
The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it is only that one dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and all will be transparently clear.
If you can find rest here, you may then cease your formal study; what further matter remains? A single word or half-phrase from the ancients is like taking a hundred...
It is as if a twenty-jin burden were placed upon your shoulders. If you are a man of true character, you would simply lift it and go, never looking back or shifting your gaze.
But if you are one of those dull-witted sorts, you will instead ask: "What is in this burden of yours?"
What kind of thing is this? It is something that cannot even be shouldered. This is a path where there is no room for you to deliberate with the mouth or ponder with the mind.
By the time you blink your eyes, where has it gone? A swift man needs but one word; a swift horse needs but one lash.
Even that is already distressing; how much more so at seventy-three or eighty-four? What can be done? A straw sandal strikes right in the mouth.
This is not beyond your capacity. To live and die together is what is called "total presentation. Whether behind the feet or before the feet, what bowl are you seeking?
You, Monk Cheng, have spent two summers gathered at Cold Spring with a single-minded resolve to discern the Way.
I wonder, have you ever investigated and practiced in this manner? Do not merely roll about within the realm of mind and nature; on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, it will not suffice.
This is a matter of realization. It is like a person eating rice: one must ask oneself whether one is hungry or full; how could another person know this?

Only when your eyes open at a later time will you believe that this old monk did not speak recklessly. He has bound the men and women of this household in iron shackles. Exert yourselves! Exert yourselves!
The Dharma words for the Venerable Master Cheng:
When the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is as if one has lost one’s parents. When the Great Matter is already clarified, it is as if one has lost one’s parents.

What was the intention behind the ancients’ such instruction? You must know that throughout the entire universe and the great earth, there is not even so much as a single mustard seed that is not [this].

At the moment when a person casts off their body and surrenders their life, a man of resolve must clench his teeth and, regardless of the passage of years or months, investigate until he reaches the bottom.
Even if one reaches the state where words do not issue as sound and forms do not appear as objects, this is still not the ultimate point.
To call it such is merely the joy of the path; one has not yet arrived home. Only by flinging open the locks of the golden hall and knocking against the jade pillars can one truly enter.
The temple bell is also a temporary play within samādhi. You must completely cast away all that you cherish in your breast—what are called jade fragments and gold coins.
Only when a great man no longer prizes these things does he become a man of the Way who has nothing to do.
This is the path for one who has no need for the medicinal arrows used against illness. Think on this, think on it!
The Dharma Words for Elder Shou of Changzhou:
The Mind-Source of all Buddhas. This mind does not exist externally. The secret intent of the Patriarchs lies right here with you.

A person of superior faculties and sharp intelligence, upon hearing a single mention of it, seizes the moment and acts; yet they still fear mistaking orange peel for fire. How [could this be otherwise]?
How much less can one deliberate or reflect upon it? "What shall I do?"—even boiling *huanglian* with its roots is not yet bitter.
An iron ox does not eat the grass by the stall; how could a butterfly long for its old nest? You must rouse your spirit and act directly upon the occasion.
When you need to use it, use it. Death is right before your eyes. See the road as you mount the horse; borrow a hand to strike a fist. Just so!
To be thus is not to be thus. Like a lion emerging from its lair, a single roar causes all beasts to vanish into silence;
this is not done by force, for such is the nature of the Dharma. Or, as one who is a traveler on the road to Jinzhou, it is difficult to speak of this.
Elder Shou has newly received the appointment to Yunju and has requested a word regarding this scroll; I shall provide it with a swift hand.
A Dharma Talk for Chan Practitioner Shiqian:
In practicing Chan, one must penetrate the barrier of the Patriarchs. A wondrous awakening requires that the path of the mind be utterly severed.

If the barrier of the Patriarchs is not penetrated and the path of the mind is not severed, you are much like a dead man whose soul has not yet dispersed; what use is there in such a state? Have you not seen how Bajiao addressed the assembly?
The Master said: "If you have a staff, I give you a staff; if you have no staff, I take your staff away.
You fabricating monks mostly engage in calculating and speculating regarding these matters of giving and taking, having and not having—yet even in a donkey’s lifetime you will not have dreamed of it.
Setting aside for a moment this matter of having, not having, giving, and taking: what do you call a staff? Right here!
There is a pearl in the eye; without moving a muscle or altering one’s expression, he captured the old fellow Bājiāo.
Fenyang also said, "If you recognize this staff, the business of a lifetime of study is finished. But how do you recognize the staff? It is a piece of coarse, rustic wood;
those with eyes see it. Now I ask you: what is the business of study? The yellow-headed and green-skinned...
"Eye! All you old monks of the world, upon reaching this point, must all be left utterly bewildered. This mountain monk says: 'To employ [wisdom], there is no need for a double-edged sword;
to prolong one's life, why rely on the nine-fold elixir? If Wei Chi does not stay at home, he dies; how could a lion ever eat a rabbit?"
Regarding the Dharma Words for General Secretary Xi:
When Kāśyapa Mātanga first entered the Han lands, he transmitted only the scriptural teachings; it was only after the "Old Barbarian" [Bodhidharma] crossed the sea that the Chan school emerged.
This is what is meant by the "separate transmission outside the teachings. Now tell me: what is it that is transmitted?
You must know that this single grasp is as light as a goose feather, yet as heavy as Mount Tai. Only those great men possessed of true strength can bear its weight.
It has been authentically inherited, continuing on without interruption. Therefore, after the predecessors awakened to the mind, they stirred it thoroughly until it became one undifferentiated whole.

His entire being is indestructible. With his three robes girded about his waist, he dwells among the mountains wherever he may be. Eating wood and wearing grass, he tills the soil with a blade and sows by fire.
Beside his hoe, he seeks out one or two companions so that this "little bundle" of practice continues without interruption.
This is not merely a scheme for his own personal peace; were it otherwise, it would be like a donkey carrying a unicorn's horn or a sheep wearing a tiger's skin.
To regard those with yellow heads and blue eyes as rare treasures and to peddle such things like petty merchants is not enough to even stain one's lips or teeth.

General Secretary, having been among the assembly for many years, you have diligently pursued the Way and do not fall into this category. It so happened that when Jiangchuan Monastery’s seat became vacant, [you were appointed].
The Prefect has sent a letter, inviting me from afar. His noble intention is clear: as the ancients said, one does not choose between the size of the monastery or the number of the assembly;
it simply depends on what one is oneself. As our late master said, "In all things, preserve this Way; in all flavors, trust in past karma.
One can see from this how the predecessors walked the truth and practiced sincerity. If you can truly practice these ten characters, [you will succeed].
The duties of a lifetime are hereby concluded. There remains one further phrase that does not involve paper or ink; it is already in a state of disorder, so you must strive with all your might.
This is the Dharma discourse shown to the Scribe Ke.
Traveling monks leave one monastery to enter another, parting the weeds and observing the wind to discern the Way, undaunted by cold or heat;
this is called "investigating Zen. But in the end, how does one investigate Zen?

If you tilt your head and strain your ears toward the old bones on the meditation seat, you will spend your entire life at seventy-three or eighty-four years, having been deceived all along. If you follow the manuals of the ancient worthies...
Searching upward, one finds those who feed on human saliva and spittle. Amidst ten thousand miles of white clouds, there are occasionally those who have resolved their will;
though they may be diligent, arduous, and fierce in their practice—three times by day and three times by night—they do not recognize the root source.

They sit within the ghost caves beneath Black Mountain, in a state of dark obscurity with no prospect of emerging. As the ancients said: "Constantly present within the moment; when recognition is exhausted, the function is perfected. In a sudden flash...
To give rise [to such thoughts] is itself to harm others. Why not rely on the instructions handed down by the ancients? Look closely with your own eyes:
coarse food satisfies easily, while fine chewing prevents hunger. As Master Xuansha said: "I have studied together with the Old Śākyamuni."
A monk then asked, "I wonder, whom have you studied under? Xue pointed to himself and said, "Xie Sanlang on the fishing boat.
This can truly be called "real brass not being worth even a fraction of gold. If students truly wish to practice Chan, this is the foremost model.
Why not investigate it in this manner? Record-keeper Ke traveled with him through the mountains north and south for many years.
It is not only that you harbor such thoughts regarding the Way; furthermore, I have read books of both ancient and modern times.
As for all the aforementioned complications of this mountain monk—tell me, within the Five Classics and the Seventeen Histories, has there ever been any such news? If you say there is:
In that regard, one phrase is sufficient. If you say there is none, there are ultimately no two paths under heaven. Just look in this way;
suddenly, when you bite your own tongue, the matter of seeking your parents will be resolved. Hurry back and reveal it; the mountain monk has another instruction for you.
Dharma Words for the Zen Practitioner Xiang:
"The Unlocalized True Person is a Dry Shit-Plug. In the Great Tang Empire there are no Zen masters. This is a ready-made case; yet you refuse to accept it.
Ten thousand miles of mountains and rivers—you have traveled them in vain. A sharp-witted monk returns at a single call. Carrying a board across one's shoulders...
"O Master, three thousand li away, Xuefeng merely asked, 'What is this? Zhaozhou treated them all alike by calling out, 'Come, have some tea.
If it concerns the *siddhārtha*—the matter of one's fundamental practice—you must realize it through your own self-acceptance; it is not something I know."
A Dharma Talk for the Junior Monk Shigu at the Multi-Child Stupa:
A pure breeze sweeps across the earth; on the road to Caoxi, the wild grasses reach to the heavens.

Those who have not undergone bitter toil do not know this. One must carve one’s own belly with one’s own hand. This is where the blind donkey grazes—treading and trampling with total freedom. The earthworm...
A frog eats mud and eats earth; yet you wish further to seek words and follow phrases—you will fall alive into the Avīci Hell.
Even if you could produce sounds like jade striking gold, it would still have nothing to do with the matter. The secret instructions of the immortals are truly worth cherishing;
though father and son are close, they cannot be transmitted.
The Recorded Sayings of Venerable Shitennō, Volume Three;
The Recorded Sayings of Venerable Shitennō, Volume Four;
Praises of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Regarding the "Manifestation of Leaving the Mountains": before he had left the mountains, the winds from the four quarters were hushed and still; as soon as he emerged from the mountains, great waves surged across the level plains.
What use is there in capturing such an ugly demeanor? It would be better to unfurl it for a long time and burn three *qian* of incense according to one's means.
The fragrance of the incense on the tower wafts into his nostrils;
when energetic, he practices walking meditation, and when weary, he sits in dhyāna. For forty-nine years, he has spent his time contemplating and committing such a multitude of verbal transgressions.
Opening his eyes with such majesty—this merely results in empty talk. A vast, pure breeze comes from the treetops;
how many can truly realize this right here? Guanyin.

Entering right concentration and practicing right contemplation, I think: "Sentient beings suffer; how can my heart find peace? Appearing in forms according to their kind, they cannot be found anywhere.
Like the heavens' wind rolling over the sea, the night waves are cold.

Hearing sounds, there is nothing heard; seeing forms, this is not seeing. Seated in meditative equipoise upon the *pāṇḍava*, neither fixed nor distracted, the entire great earth is fully realized as perfect penetration.
Only then do I fulfill my compassionate vow to deliver sentient beings.

Avalokiteśvara contemplates that the ocean of suffering is deep and his compassionate vows are vast. He reflects thus: "By what skillful means can I cause all sentient beings everywhere to reach the other shore?"

The maiden of the horse-herd is pure and true in both voice and form; she is unimpeded by what is seen or heard. Whether in seated meditation or walking practice, she attains great mastery. From head to toe, her feet are dark and vast;
once again, she follows the spring wind as the wife of the horse-herd.

Bodhidharma’s flawless white jade was cast into the darkness; he encountered others who drew their swords against him. He broke off a stalk of reed and returned to face the surging waves; though the entire nation pursued him, he would not turn back.
To conceal his shame, he relied on the presence of Master Xian.

I am a man from the eastern lands. My nature was originally pure and true, yet it has been shattered by that "clarity," not worth half a coin. Skin, flesh, bone, and marrow lie in a chaotic mess of contention.
Had I been able to take this medicine and die then, today I would surely have seen an era of Great Peace.
He arrived at the Liang dynasty in a reckless manner, yet failed to accord with the intent of the Liang court. Letting him pass with one stroke, he fled into the territory of Wei.
Although Shen Guang spoke of "settling the mind," he could not avoid losing an arm.

The First Patriarch crossed the seas and braved the desert sands to come; how many times did his medicine fail to kill? It has ruined the people of this land of China, who remain mired in sickness and confusion to this day.

The Second Patriarch sought his mind but found no place to seek it; at that very moment, his mind was at peace. Had he known earlier that ice is water, his two arms would certainly have remained intact.
The Third Patriarch...
When seeking the offense, it cannot be found; where else could one repent? The clouds and mists suddenly part, and the solitary moon rises in the clear blue sky.
Fourth Patriarch, who binds you? No one binds you. Why seek liberation further? It may not necessarily be the geese of Wang Xizhi; they might simply be the cranes of Zhi Loukajia.

The Fifth Patriarch planted pine trees that now fill the mountains. In secret, he turned his body around. Although he obtained the robe of faith, how could he have known his father’s face?—the Sixth Patriarch.
At the waist-stone and the mortar-house, he pounds grain; he does not recognize a single stroke of a character. There are no trees and no platforms, yet the bowl-bag is still passed down.

Carrying a cloth bag on a staff, clouds arise beneath his feet. Through the streets before and the alleys behind, there is no record or trace at all; he calls out, patting the back of one who can be summoned.
Return! How many people can grasp this talk? For now, one can only do what must be done. It is difficult to transform the people of Tiefeng and Huacheng;
they decline the invitation of Tuṣita Heaven and mingle within the mundane dust. Last night, with eyes closed, my belly was wide awake.
How about getting up now, taking up the staff, and walking east and west? Suddenly, wait and watch for such a person.
Begging for money, yet there is no money; looking for people, yet no one is seen. Who knows how the Tuṣita Heaven compares to the Hanging Rock of Fenghua?
Clapping hands and laughing "he-he"—the heavens turn and the earth revolves!
The portraits of Fenggan, Hanshan, and Shide:
among these three, there must be a teacher for me. Stinking meat is originally of one flavor. Holding hands and gathering their heads together: *sulū sili*.
It was simply because they were the first to be talkative; now these two have no place to hide themselves.
It is a pity that back then at Guoqing Temple there was a whole crew of dull-witted monks who lacked even a trace of intelligence.
In the first scene of the Four Sleeps Diagram, two men come riding tigers, shoulder to shoulder. Outside the pine gate, they huddle their heads together and roll into one place to sleep.
Dreaming of the butterfly, they are so enraptured they do not know who is the man and who is the tiger. Wait until their eyes open—then look at the South Mountain!
There is a turning phrase:
"Fahua treads wooden sandals and points at empty space; the *dharmaparyāya-samādhi* has a resonant root of the tongue. These thirteen characters are written in succession.
Like insects boring through wood, they have drawn in a class of heterodox followers who, to this day, continue their wild and confused conjectures.

Hanshan and Shide—whether carving poems upon wooden leaves while gazing at the moon, or serving as kitchen attendants tending the hearth—seized leisure during the night to stroll and relax amidst the forest; they were like a single, pure vessel of ice.

There is no reflection; he clearly pierces through their very liver and gallbladder. It is laughable that at that time on Mount Tiantai, not a single person possessed the true eye—not even Pig-Headed Monk.
Holding a pig’s head in his hand, it is easy to see but difficult to recognize; do not let him speak of it, for it is not worth a single coin.
Master Xianni held up a ladle for scooping up waves, exhausting every last trick he had; he pushed out the wine tray, yet to this day it has not been reclaimed.
Master Yangqi did not understand Chan, yet he still presided over a monastery. He possessed no realization at all; he merely farmed the land to trade for his meals.

With a great laugh, he received Baiyun, that blind fellow, who pointlessly brought misfortune upon his descendants throughout the land. To this day, people cannot distinguish east from west, nor discern north from south.
In the *Record of Master Wuzu Fayan*, it says:
"Even after ten years of study, you have not yet seen it; only upon catching a glimpse of Baiyun did you finally penetrate it.

Indeed, there was one who surpassed his master. I dare say that Elder Master Duan’s words were clumsy: he lived his entire life in Huai and never entered Zhejiang, yet he alone played with this single, raised point. Until—

In the lineage that received the three Buddhas and governed the Southern Hall, a single great treasury was transmitted to Chiruanyafu; this is what is called the "Orthodox Continuation of the Eastern Mountain" (Dongshan Zhengxu).
It has not shifted by so much as a hair’s breadth throughout ten million generations, possessing a profound source and a long-reaching stream.
Master Puhua roamed through the city walls, shaking his bell. He ate raw vegetables in the courtyard; when he encountered a donkey, its temper flared.
He exposed the wooden pagoda of Heyang and captured the lowly soldier Linji. He deceived the people of the entire city of Zhenzhou. The sound of the bell has long since faded into the distance.
The heavens are vast.
Master Linji presses down with empty fists;
his shout thunders like a clap of thunder. Amidst the flashing lightning, he seeks to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox, yet he mounts a great fabrication.
Selling stolen goods of which no owner exists—such a heartless disposition! Yet even now, there are still those who follow;
Vimalakīrti occupies his high chair, while the wind blows in silence. Those forty-eight fools running about at night cannot avoid falling into his trap.
The Teacher of the Seven Buddhas was caught up in a chain of entanglements. At that time, Shitian was by his side; he need only have let out a single sneeze.

Lingzhao, that girl of evil stock, gave birth to an enemy. She set the price for the *yeli* (a type of woven screen) without a single coin’s deviation. In the end, she was still intolerable—her timing was sharp.
Previously he did not yield to his father.
Master Po’an was capable of nothing;
he was detested by all. He was like fishing for turtles in fire or hiding ice in the sun. He raised his son but never taught him; with a single rope...
Above, further secure the rope. This is the true lineage of Guku-dongshan.

Monk Uhuhujin of Boncheon composed this [hymn] on the Water-Moon Avalokiteśvara manifesting in a majestic and dignified form, giving rise to a heart of compassion for the benefit of others: "The waters are vast and boundless; the moon is deep and serene. Sentient beings..."
It is inexhaustible; my vow is just beginning. Dawn turns back to dusk; past, present, and future are obliterated.

I join Fenggan as he hastens through the pines to seek Hanzhu and Shishi. The tiger’s stripes are easy to see, but the human stripes are difficult to recognize. Whether recognized or not, there is but an evil reputation.
The traces left behind were in utter disarray.

Zhan [Fengyan] carried his bag, acting like one driven mad by the wind as he ran through the marketplace. Turning his head, he looked back; leaning his staff across his shoulder, the mountain monk saw him and could not help but...
No words. [囗@力]. Set down the tattered cloth bag. I give you one coin. Praise for the Three Teachings Diagram Warning the World’s Ignorance:
Three Old Men. Though their garments differ, their hearts are the same. To deliberate on their relative superiority or inferiority is like shooting with a weed-arrow.
In the void, Huangniu (the Yellow Ox) does not understand how to ride backward;
he follows wherever the ox leads. Across the level plains of the outskirts, neither whip nor tether is employed. The mountains grow dark and the waters...
Wyi-wyi. Those who know me are the white egrets.
The immortal gazes at the moon, washing his feet;
the night is still, the mountains empty, the moon a half-crescent. He pulls up his robes and lowers his feet to cleanse them in the murmuring stream. No one understands this profound depth.
The Master said, "Go separately into the jar and look for the deity yourself.
Zanzong Daozhe ran down to Tongcheng and returned barefoot; he was half mad and half foolish, wearing his straw sandals upon his *kāṣāya*.
A bundle. Two tigers and a pair of crows laugh him to death.
Praising Master Huangbo’s “true pearl wrapped in coarse cloth”:
dwelling in an ancient temple, he joyfully maintains his simplicity; he gave the name "Peaceful" to Duke Pei, and faced Baizhang, he stuck out his tongue.
Striking out a tiny infant from the tip of the staff, he then had a sudden flash of insight beneath Dayu’s words. Whether it was a flash or not, he was struck with a single palm;
how can this be cleared away?

In praise of the Man in the Straw Raincoat, who feigns madness to blend with the world and nourish his harmony with Heaven: though the celestial realms are as crowded as government offices, through summer he passes into winter, and from winter back into summer;
outside that single straw raincoat, there is nothing else.
Praising the morning sun as it pierces through his tattered robe; waiting for the moon to finish his incomplete sutra.
A single robe for three winters, woven with thousands of needles and ten thousand threads. When the sunlight has risen three spans high, his eyesight has increased by half.
The sun’s shadow has already passed; my sutra remains unfinished. Closing the volume, I stand for a brief moment. An ice-clear pitcher hangs from the treetops.

Elder Fu requested a eulogy for a portrait of the Master, pledging to bestow it without violating his command, using it as medicine against illness. Since the time of the Patriarchs, there have been many who have misunderstood; they take the patch-robed monk...
His precious wealth has been completely confiscated; empty of virtue yet puffed up with pride, he has spent years without merit. Among them all, one person is most pitiable:
his carriage is being pushed crosswise onto the road. (Shame!)
Elder Li of Chaozhou requests a eulogy for his face, which is like dead ashes;
it cannot be lifted by a spoon. He has utterly squandered the ancestral patrimony.
Yet, when he picks up a scale without weights, he still knows how to distinguish pounds and ounces. Elder Li reflects deeply; fortunately, the crocodiles have moved on and transformed.
He lured him back, only to bring about disaster.

He praises himself for living in a state of dull indifference and acting with careless haste when faced with affairs. He is far too down-to-earth; people call him an "old man," and now his reputation for being right or wrong has reached my ears.
The wind blows through the stone mortar; it remains as it is, yet this is most unseemly. One who can ride a three-legged donkey travels the roads of Chang’an.
Elder Zhang invites a eulogy.
Capable of nothing among the hundred arts, his face as cold as ice, he stands aloof from the world, drifting freely and at ease.
He took up the "Single-Word Zen" and toppled the monk Du; Elder Chushan, however, insisted on receiving its transmission. Gu, Gu, Gulin, and Zhenzhen.
Each has its own resonance; why then must it be written down? There is no gold here.

Elder Kaccāna, you have requested a praise, yet a blade does not cut itself, nor does water wash itself. How can it be logical for me to praise myself? Since his request was so insistent, [he complied].
He refused it repeatedly. There is one phrase that Xuan Sha spoke from the depths:
"Master Qing'an requested a eulogy for [a field] made of stone;
the whole world laughed at this as strange. A single grain enters the earth and, without weeding, it flourishes of itself. There is no Zen, either."
There is no Way. Even before a monk has stepped through the gate, he has already been thoroughly scrutinized. Within the crown of his head, there is naturally a passage that pierces the heavens.
(A shout! Elder Zhao requests a eulogy for the state of having no apertures at all.
Pointing to mulberry trees while scolding willows, he blinds the true eye of the monk and breaks the secret code of Dongshan. Three dots.
After the first three points, the pattern has already been set without end; let others at their leisure debate its beauty or ugliness.
The Layman of Cold Rock requests a eulogy for an ignorant old bhikṣu of the Dharma-ending age:
seeking seams in empty space, he rows a boat on land. The Layman of Cold Rock may indeed be said to possess such a heart and mind.
Poisonous! To write this out is to provoke endless reproach.
The Elder Nun invited me to reside at the mountain for thirty years;
my vigor has faded and my karmic fortune is meager. When I fully present this one point, the patch-robed disciples knit their brows. I have none.
As for the work of Master Guishan: you possess the faculty of the iron-grinding wheel; you know yourself that it is difficult to fish for the moon at the bottom of the water.
Yet you have asked me to employ brush and ink to defile it.
Elder Xiu requests a eulogy.
Beneath Feilai Peak, by the corner of the dragon bed, he employs a move devoid of intention; thus, the master-monks are deluded and distracted by him.

Suddenly, the *huqin* flute turns to the melody of "Yangchun"; there is one who knows the music coming to join as a companion. Yet even if one were to attempt to depict this, it would not reach even half of it.
Even if this story were to flourish greatly at this very moment, it would already be a situation where neither party finds any advantage.
In praise of the portraits of Li Yuan and Yuanze:
Though their spirits are vivid and manifest, they have not yet escaped birth and death. To encounter this wretched kinsman by chance on a narrow path—how can one bear it?
The "Song of Summoning the Horn" before the mountains of India still lingers in its lingering resonance among the pines and vines to this day.
I praise Master Lü:

as a Confucian, he did not succeed in Confucianism; as one who studied the Way of the Immortals, the immortality he sought was not real. Passing beneath the gate of the Yellow Dragon, he was like an autumn mosquito biting an iron nail.
"Master Huí, Master Huí! A man of Yuéyáng who does not recognize him; an old tree that has become a spirit.
The Layman Ju-shi of Jiào-chéng requests a eulogy for the Master’s portrait:
entirely devoid of even an inch of merit, he simply follows his 'donkey-nature. He does not travel to the bottom of the deep sea, nor does he stand atop the highest peak."
Questioning the Buddha-dharma: today I am weary; it blinds the eyes of the blind monks. You recognize the illness of Vaiśālī; originally you have no enmity with the City of Enlightenment.
For what reason do you depict his form and paint his likeness?

At the request of the disciple of my dharma-teacher’s grandson, I composed this eulogy for the tonsure ceremony at a village monastery. Being a woman of meager appearance and little learning, I have followed my feet to the southern lands and likewise become a mountain-dwelling nun.
Idle talk from the corner of the dragon-bed has drawn in monks like swarming bees. Longing for home yet unable to go, dreams of my native land come frequent.
"I earnestly entrust you to carry me away"—just look at the pear blossoms in the spring of the second month (at my place of study in Pear Blossom Village).
I praise myself: others discard what I take up; others seize what I give. My engagement with the world is entirely contrary; I walk alone without a companion.
This "head-on phrase" that transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs—the Cold Spring flows on day and night. With hands folded, one hesitates to speak while sitting in a secluded place—how pitiful!
Defiled by rouge and vermilion;
grasping a whisk and sitting upon a rope seat, he remains silent and speechless. His voice rings out clearly, severing the life-vein of the monks and destroying the discipline of the monastic groves.
Painted in vivid colors, his ugliness is impossible to conceal; let others at their leisure discuss his merits and faults.
The verse says:
A poisonous fruit on an iron tree blooms in the dead of night; Upon its branches it forms a round, clustered seed. From ancient times to the present, this medicine has killed people without end.
Counting. One who does not believe the teaching bites through it to see.
The patriarch who sold firewood was originally just a firewood seller; today he has no firewood, and how pitiable! It would be well to go visit the donor’s gate and gather [the wood].
Picking up [the staff], he returns intending to meet the smoke of the midday meal.
Sending off Guishi An back to Shu (composed while serving as Head Seat at Jingci Temple):
In the past you followed the current; now you go against it. There is a reason for what was then and what is now. General Li was originally one who could pierce the willow leaves.
With his hand, he mistakenly shot a stone at the South Mountain;
the hearth and cauldron were transformed and already cast without leakage. While the hearth is not yet built, he is still busily engaged in the work. Lay down your staff, O Master of Songshan!
He comes forth. I desire the fragrance of congee to be heard at the fifth watch.
Sending off Chanter Zong to take charge of the monastery:
upon the banks of the Tongjiang River, a single thread of wind blows; he does not fish for blind turtles, but only for dragons. Who can discern the presence or absence of his floating samādhi?
It is late at night; the coolness is like water, the moon is like a bow.
I have gone up to Zhangji’s Hermitage to beg for rice, yet the rice fences of Nanshan are empty these days.
It is difficult to teach the patch-robed monks to suck the wind from their mouths. I stretch out my arm toward the upper realm of the Fragrant Accumulation.
The realm: one must labor with golden millet to display spiritual powers;

to receive guests, one fills the steamer with cooked rice made from no grain. To welcome those who do not come halfway along the road—one simply holds this saying to circulate throughout all quarters.
Depart! To know the resonance of the distant is a new smile.
Inscribed on the Stupa of Lei Qian at Shishuang:

A single thought of compassionate countenance is fundamentally not separated [from us]. Why need one deliberately act with such eccentricity? Leveling the high and conforming to the low is the compassionate heart.
Truly vexing, it left the Thunder God busy all night long.
I offer this verse of my own:
Plowing fields upon stony ground is rare in this world; even the old farmer frowns when he hears of it. If there is someone who can descend into the Avīci Hell...
A variety of fragrant offerings were prepared in separate steamers for his service.
He sent Shao Heshang to manage the restoration of the foundations of Lingyun’s ancient temple;
the swordsman sought it out again, yet the cataracts of his eyes had grown. To this day, the solitary exposure remains unbearable to hear; Old Shao was able to support him directly beneath.
Arise! The spirit of ten mouths has diminished by eight parts;
he turns his body with a laugh inside the great furnace of the bell and cauldron. With an empty stomach and a haughty mind, he promises tenfold success; listen well as the Jade Tower strikes.
The place: sending forth a harmonious voice with too much clarity.
Sending Jiao Zhong’an to dwell at Guangshou;
his name’s fragrance fills the roads. He draws the waters of Dong back to pour into Nanhu. In time, he will come here holding his staff lightly.
Investigate! Do not say that there has never been a single drop from the past.

When the Head Seat Yue was sent to dwell in a hermitage, he bound grass together to make his hut—a practice of the sages of old. Throughout antiquity and today, who comes after and who comes before? When a guest arrives, one must be able to respond with universal mastery.
Verse: Do not merely follow along with the heterodox by raising your fist.

As you escort the Venerable Guī back to his home, the Southern High Peak faces the Northern High Peak; these two peaks stand tall, reaching up to touch the azure heavens. The Venerable One has set down his staff there.
Down! Biting ginger and drinking vinegar, one anticipates the emptiness of the mind. When the mind is empty, there is not a single thing upon which to rely.

Yet they laugh at the Old Barbarian for pointing his fingers in a crooked way; turning their heads, they seek once more the mountains of their former home. Do not follow my example by wandering through the overgrown weeds.
Wu Daofu begs for words;
his feet stumble along until his two sandals are worn through. The scrolls upon his shoulder he has yet to cast aside.
Wait until you have suffered the illness of Vimalakīrti, and then it will be well for you to come again to see Shitian.
I bid farewell to Master Chao:
A single point of numinous light penetrates everywhere; when the mind is empty, even the great void cannot be seen.
To take five thousand words as profound and mysterious—how can damp paper wrap a tiger?
To the Monk Yunsang of Jizhou:
In speech and movement, you are entirely natural. Folding your hands is but a vain effort to question others. It is said that the wine of the Bai family was once served at Qingyuan;
now that you have returned home, take care not to touch its lips again.
The Three Verses in the Calligraphy of He Zhenxie:
This matter completely transcends the vast eons; To clarify the position by means of function is not in vain.
Provided one does not offend the father’s taboo name, The moon may freely be full wherever it goes.
Resounding, the myriad phenomena embody the primal truth; Rained upon and steamed by clouds, they appear fresh before the eyes. I fear that opening my mouth would lead to falling into categories;
Yet when we meet, for the most part, we simply smile and laugh.

Casting off one's hands while suspended over a ten-thousand-fathom cliff—only then does one know that for Buddhas and Patriarchs there are no ladders or steps. Without cause, the various elders vie to display their ugliness;
they cannot avoid burying themselves in a single spot.
The nun was clearly capable and resourceful;
she requested instructions and circumambulated the meditation seat three times before her eyes had even opened. She rose to take up the brush and paper to draft a model for arrangement.
Once the tangled vine of the teaching pillar is perfected, the dragons and devas will naturally lend a hand with their mallets.
At the Tea Ceremony, I beg for a verse:
The mind has neither low nor high; In this single state of no-mind, one pours the tea in succession. This is precisely swallowing the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
To receive even a single drop of it is difficult to digest.
A hundred thousand households march out from within the city;
the imperial capital is vast and deep. At the mere thought of Nan Shan, one reaches the very marrow of one's bones in poverty.
Layer upon layer of iron walls are pushed through; a handleless colander scoops up the spring breeze.
The monk who severed his arm reclaimed his fields and estates.
When the ancients severed their arms to seek peace of mind, how could there be anything they possessed that we do not? A master among masters boasts of his mastery;
the eternal presence of a thousand years rests upon a single morning’s monk.
I present this iron whip from Shaozhou to West Yu;
West Yu was formerly called Duan Shizi. How many people nowadays can truly perform it? This is not a mere matter of empty courtesy;
you must witness the hand-eye coordination all at once.
Seeing off a monk:
After a long drought, half the fields in Wu have failed to yield. You are now heading from West Zhejiang to East Zhou. For now, you seek a place where your cooking cloth may be unfurled;
let the Buddha-dharma rot away as it pleases.
To send off Zen student Yuan:
At Mount Ling, there is no place for the body to rest; it is better to sail upon the river tides to seek the ford. The monastic groves of Eastern Zhejiang are as vast as the sea;
simply investigate the pillar of dew, and do not investigate people.

The fried bamboo shoots have just shed their brocade-like skins to reveal jade-white flesh; yet they are further treated with oil-frying for his sustenance. How much salt and vinegar has been wasted for him!
His tongue has been exchanged, yet he remains unaware.
The physiognomist Zhu Shuoyi has eyes that have seen the world and possess their own divine power. When wine drenches his breast, his speech brings forth the spirit of spring.
Within his single straw cloak lies a vast universe; do not hastily speak of it to others.
Master Kong begs for a verse on Cold Spring:
"Recently the rice baskets have been empty; alas, the harvest has not come this year.
There is a wondrous prescription for abstaining from grain, which monks vied with one another to ask of Tiantong."
The Venerable Chief Preceptor Hei, styled Shitan, stares with wide-open eyes at the azure heavens.
He devours Buddhas and patriarchs raw, his spirit bold and majestic. Who can fathom the depths of Shitan?
All day long, the golden wind stirs up raging waves.
Seeing Master Zhao Return to Shu:
I fell into this southern journey with hair already gray; how can you now regret coming late? With your black staff clattering, you return to that place;
let the Buddhas and Patriarchs have no cause to knit their brows.
Presented to Master Yungok:
Turning the lines upon the divination board to savor the workings of Heaven’s mechanism. Calamity has its embryo; fortune has its foundation.
Last night the planet Pei shifted one position, yet the Master slept soundly and remained unaware.
The Patriarchal Ancestors have transmitted it from one to another until the present day; heaven is high and earth is distant, and those who truly understand it are few.
When people arrive home and ask about this transmission, simply say: "True brass does not trade for gold."
A monk of the Huashan school took his blood, mixed it with ink, and transcribed the Tripiṭaka, seeking verses for the old scriptures to be written after the fire.
He scraped his blood and mixed it with soot; every single character was authentic. Before he had even raised his brush, the entire Canon was complete.
Hearing the strings of this lute, there must surely be one who can appreciate the sound.
The Vinaya Master Bin contended for the fields;
the monk’s public warrant is already clear. He strove with all his might for the ancestral gardens and fields; one day, the water and clouds shall bring equal satiety.
How many, having set down their chopsticks, forget this kindness?
Master Duan’s gate was steep and lofty;
as an old tree at Mount Shan, his pure wind was chilling and truly difficult to scale. From ancient times to the present, there has been no gap between this and that;
it lies only within the turn of one's own hand.
Send this young disciple on his travels;
do not refuse the physical exertion required to visit all quarters. The Buddha-dharma is not vast, yet it requires long-term cultivation.
Having traversed every rugged path, one reaches level ground; upon returning, overturn the broken meditation seat.
The sword-blade turned over before the assembly is still dull; asking for directions at one's own roof is utterly groundless. A chicken of Chu is no phoenix of Mount Dan;
why must it preen its feathers against the wind?
Master Bǐng returns to his hometown; his style name is Nánshān (South Mountain).
Years have passed as he drifted like a cloud over rivers and seas. Once, at Wǔfēng, he realized the pivot of Shàolín. His "white-handed" thievery truly surpasses that of his master.
I shall join him in taking Nánshān back with him.
Send Xiaoran back to his hometown;
travel to distant lands early, and return home early. One must practice Zen while still young.
Let not bystanders laugh at you lightly; Linji originally called him the "little sick child."
Presented to Chan Guest Tong for Questioning the Dharma at the Dragon Steps, which moved the Emperor’s countenance: the Emperor bestowed ten thousand coins of gold.
Having struck out the monk’s official seal of verification, Chan Guest Tong remains, as always, just Chan Guest Tong.

I see off my dharma-grandson, the monk Mei, who became a monk at fifteen and returned home at twenty; his journey is incomparable to his time at home. I, this old monk, remain here in Zhejiang while you return to Shu;
the three samādhis have been thus from of old, and no one has known them.
Leaving Jingci Temple for Lingyin, he firmly guards the pass upon the lake.
Solitary and precarious, standing alone, there is no way to climb further. Lacking the power of concentration in old age, he turns with the wind;
once more he passes from the South Mountain to the North Mountain.
Inscription on the Two Circular Diagrams by Lord Lou, Minister of State Affairs;

written by Jiao Ran with the characters "Ping" (Level) and "Ding" (Settled). Gongkui has transcribed these two circular diagrams, thereby leading countless ordinary people to gaze at clouds and climb trees.
For now, let us rejoice that both have no connection [to the truth]. Yet, if one wishes to know the reality, one must personally see Shitian.
Regarding the authentic calligraphic manuscript of Baozhenxie,

the "Letter to His Compassionate Mother" by Old Man Baozhenxie, and the various inscriptions and colophons from different quarters— each expresses its own perspective, and thus they differ from one another.
Little do they realize that the letter itself states: "If this is a reply, there should naturally be a separate sheet.

Furthermore, the mention of having received the imperial decree to reside in the mountains, as well as inquiries regarding his kinsmen and dependents, reflects the ultimate affection between mother and son; why, then, should one harbor any resentment?
How could it be necessary for every word to speak of transcending the world before it may be considered appropriate? Students ought to seek the truth in this.
Inscription on the Calligraphy of Wan’an:
Wan’an gathers flowers from within emptiness; everyone else plants lotus roots upon stones. Three dots before, three dots after—moving the Southern Star and missing the Northern Dipper.
This mountain monk’s mouth is like a stone millstone; the deity Śūnyatādeva must have lost his laughter.
Regarding the colophon for the transcription of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by the layman He:
The Great Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* is the ultimate discourse among all sutras. A single character contains ten thousand dharmas; a single sound pervades all things.

To deliberate upon it with the mouth or contemplate it with the mind is like wrapping fire in damp paper. Layman He has transcribed this and bestowed it upon various famous mountains, so that those with the karmic affinity may open it and recite it. It is not... [end of fragment].
He comes from among the fifty-three encounters with elders and laypeople; how could he be otherwise?
If one does not give rise to even a single thread of intellectual understanding beyond the black characters on white paper, then one may approximate the realm of the Great Man.
The Dharma has three cycles and seven parables.
[The Buddha] repeatedly declined with firm words, refusing to speak easily; yet, through persistent and earnest entreaty, he made the opening and exposition of the teaching his ultimate goal.
Having no choice, he opened the eight characters wide to fulfill the expectations of the fourfold assembly. [Endorsement by Wan Shan You upon the transcription of the Lotus Sūtra]
I long for this. O virtuous friend, Wanjun: the bamboo slips and ink, the hair-tip brush and the polished inkstone, all possess the potential for Buddhahood;
these silver hooks and iron strokes shall surely gather the essentials for aiding the Teaching. This is the most supreme of causes and conditions—how could it be a minor merit?
I possess a great scripture, its measure equal to the vast void; its essential features are revealed directly before one’s eyes.
Only upon paper does it become stained and defiled.
For the sake of Chan practitioner Xin, Vice Director Ba-jia has carved these Buddha-verses.
When the Chan practitioner Ziyang Zongxin was still a layman, he carved stone images of the Buddha with the utmost exquisite skill.
One day, he abandoned that life, shaved his head to study the Buddha-dharma, and requested a word from the layman Cuzhai, who spoke a verse for him.

It flowed forth in a continuous, winding stream, no different from words issuing directly from the Buddha’s own mouth. I do not know whether Zongxin was able to grasp its meaning. Nevertheless, he still lacks one crucial step.
As for this, the first verse of the Layman’s [Xuedou’s] poem says: "The thousands of millions of Buddhas in one's hands / Each and every one arises from the mind.
One can surely go and ask the Layman: "I do not know from where this 'mind' of mine arises.
The Layman must certainly have another way of turning himself around; if he does not, you must by all means avoid dying under the Layman's words.
Inscription on the Calligraphy of Liu Yousi, the Shuozhai Jushi.
For the sake of the attendant Chuan, he transcribed the words of Longmen and Baiyang and presented them to me, requesting that I write a few words following them. I said:
"The speech of these two elders was upright and their words were upright; Shuozhai’s mind is correct and his brushwork is correct. You..."

One who is able to have profound faith and exert effort from this very day shall record their meritorious achievements in the sacred abode. Even a hair-tip of ink or a wash of water possesses a share of such merit; how much more so, then, for one who observes the fast on the first day of the month!
Chancellor Bao You transcribed the Heart Sūtra and the Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra for the Venerable Yin.
Each character in this transcription by the Great Grand Councilor is a single, perfect character, which the Venerable Yin has received and maintains through recitation.
Each phrase is a single phrase. Shítian dares not add a single frivolous word to slander the true meaning of the Dharma.
Chījué transcribed the Master’s discourse on the hall; Xīnchán used it to seek words from Nánshān at midnight.
Xìnjiǎo passed through Liányún with unhesitating steps; Tàibái needlessly took up his brush to pursue these old traces. Xīnchán—
People have carefully preserved this, unaware that it contains a mortal grievance between them and this mountain monk. Those who see it must not fail to clear his injustice.
A minor Buddhist service.
For the late Grand Preceptor, Prince Wei, whose spirit transcends the three realms and for whom there is no fixed dharma:
where can one seek the mind? The four great elements are fundamentally empty; one should have no place of abiding.
Therefore, our Grand Preceptor, Prince Wei, comes by virtue of the power of his vows and departs by virtue of the power of his vows, taking this coming and going as the very field of nirvana.

He treats birth and death as mere playthings. Once in a millennium, a man such as he appears; once in a hundred generations, a peerless figure arises. He holds both civil and military rank, and his beneficence covers the entire world.
Having once supported the radiant sun, he now hangs high in the azure heavens. Compared to Yi Yin, Fu Yue, Zhou Gong, and Shao Gong, he does not yield even slightly;

when set against Zhi Jun, Wei Xian, Li Linfu, Fang Xuanling, and Du Hongjian, none can rival him. As for the tradition of producing successive ministers from a ministerial lineage, his fame and brilliance are most resplendent.
Twenty-seven examinations; serving at the Zhongshu and Fenyang offices, he likewise avoided formal seats. Reaching the age of venerable longevity, he secured ultimate auspiciousness.

A fief was carved from the soil and a princely rank became hereditary—this, moreover, has never occurred since antiquity. How could it have been sought in ancient records? It is now here. Who would not feel profound grief and pain?
Having reached the rank of general or minister in his official career, he returned to his hometown in wealth and honor—a return that was previously unattainable.
Now I have finally returned; the two paths of birth-and-death are fundamentally not distinct. Since the two paths are not distinct, the ten directions run both vertically and horizontally.
From head to foot, it is the road that reaches the heavens; tread directly upon the crown of Vairocana’s head.

Acting as the witness for the torch-bearing at He-tang (on the sixteenth day of the second month), he was a true bone-descendant of Yuanwu, a son who broke up the household at Ren-tang, and a pickaxe for mountain-dwelling. He upheld the Dharma in six or seven places.

At the end of his years, he resolutely declined the invitation to the Furi Temple and returned to sweep the chambers of Mount Ling. Once again he took up the "Golden Circle" and the "Thorny Plum," driving the monk in the single robe to the very top of the wall.
When the ordinary moment arrived, he let go and lay down in the vast expanse of space; beyond the Skull Mountain, no news could pass.
On the fifteenth day, Gautama acted thus; on the sixteenth day, he likewise acted thus in the Hall. Such is his playful mastery.
Life and death: there is nothing acceptable and nothing unacceptable. There is nothing acceptable and nothing unacceptable; it is transparent and brilliant on all eight sides.
Yangqi’s donkey is mounted backward, trampling the Child of Bingding to death.
For the sake of Elder Dīpa, a single bright lamp was placed within the interior of the stupa. Three people took a tortoise and turned it into a turtle; it was all because of this *huatou*.

For ten thousand miles they rushed south and ran north; now the oil is exhausted and the lamp has gone out, and one beholds that fundamentally there is nothing. (So-and-so), since this is the fundamental...
There is nothing that comes. Now tell me, how will you deliberate upon this? Where the sun and moon do not reach, there is a particularly fine radiance.
[This is for] the cremation of Head Seat Yuan.
Behind Mount Zhongshan, we once shared a seat; before the Peak of the Wisdom Sun, we gathered our heads again. In a dream, I turned over and suddenly knew it was there:
I blow my jade flute horizontally as I pass through the blue mists of the coastal isles. Yuan, Head Seat, stay, stay! Nan-shan has a word to entrust you with once more.
Now tell me: what was entrusted? "The fire burns at the bottom of the sea; do not speak of it wrongly when meeting people.
For the sake of Elder Shaozong, as he is being committed to the flames, what is his lineage?
How does he succeed to it? At the top of a hundred-foot pole, let go with both hands—clearly clear, there is nothing more to be done.
Understood. Striking iron does not separate it from the sparks; right before one's eyes, one may leap about as one pleases.

For the sake of Senior Monk Qing, the bright pearl of Zhenhai has been utterly free of flaw, yet with his feet straddling Nan Mountain, he personally encountered its shattering. Since it has been shattered, it must...

Understand this! Should you encounter someone on the road ahead who asks for this pearl, with a single stroke of "flint-fire" beyond the blue sky, you shall overturn the Great Canon and Small Canon, the Half-month and Full-month [collections], and everything else as well. A single iron bar across ten thousand miles—just so!
This is not yet intimate. This mountain monk’s mouth is like a foundation stone; yet listen to this verbose fellow with the torch.

To distinguish the Abbot’s descent into the fire and to pour forth the Yellow River is already the second level; his mouth hangs on the wall, and the thunder shakes the earth. Within this, who can grasp it?
He set out immediately; there was not even the space of a hair’s breadth for deliberation.
Smoke rose from his feet and fire blazed from his head.
For the sake of Elder Lin, he extinguished the fire at Jiangshang and set forth; at Feilai Peak, he immediately struck down his bedding. This is a single phrase that does not involve the journey.
Son! In the midst of a mass of blazing flames, he cuts his forehead and gazes.

For the sake of Elder Dēṅ, he extinguishes the fire and does not accept the prediction of enlightenment from the lighting of the lamp. He does not seek out idle Dharmas; he breaks through the sturdy gate of birth and death with a single blow of the fist. Even if you—
It is so. Yet he has not yet let it go; one must simply see smoke from behind the mountain, rather than drilling ice to seek fire.

Because Master Zhan was unable to extinguish the fires of a minor disciple, who was beset by an illness that ultimately failed to heal, the *kuta* tally in the room was further reduced. On the other side of Mount Sumeru, the teaching is opened anew.
The Eye must be sought within the fire of refined gold.

As for the saying that "if an honored elder descends into the fire and enters through the gate, he is not the family treasure; if he does not enter through the gate, he is likewise not the family treasure"—it is thus.
To do so would be to bury the former sages; not to do so would be to betray one's own spiritual essence. O precious practitioners of Zen: when tending the furnace, one does not avoid the fire;
when spring comes, the grass grows green of its own accord.
When serving as Wen’s attendant, he descended into the fire before even attaining Buddhahood;
yet his literary brilliance was already manifest. With his skull broken through, he was free from all dependence; having leaped out, he was beyond the realm of demons and certain death.
But tell me: after leaping out, what is it like? When the *udumbara* flower blooms amidst a mass of fire, one who smells it does not perceive its fragrance.

For the sake of the Chan guest Xiu, I have engaged in many years of standing battles. His mouth and beak are full of clamor; every turn has its path, and every step ascends higher. Yet he is too hasty in his pursuit of progress.
He took this one fall. He has indeed fallen. Do you still remember yesterday’s *huatou*? [The Master] raised his fire-tongs and said:
"Though the eyebrows remain, alas, the nostrils have already been scorched."
For the sake of Dharma Master Taifa, he did not burn the verse inscribed on the wall, nor did he transmit the midnight robe. For sixty-three years he waited in vain;
now that his white hairs have grown long, the time has finally arrived and he suddenly knows where to return. He topples the shadowless tree over there and comes back to the fire.
Reprint from the Inner Section. Volume Four (End). Biographical Sketch:
The Master’s name was Faxun; his style name was Shitian. He was of the Peng clan of Meishan. He was a disciple of the late Master Xiatang Yuan of Lingyin Monastery during the Chunhua era.
During the Xihuan era, an imperial edict inquired about the Buddha-dharma;

his responses were in accord with the Emperor’s wishes, and he was granted the title Chan Master Bohai. He was of the same clan as the aforementioned ancestor. The Master was naturally gifted from birth;

at the age of three or four, upon seeing a Buddha or a monk, he immediately knew how to pay them respect. At sixteen, he earnestly requested permission from his parents to leave the household life and went to follow [Master] Shi of Danling.
Zhiming of Fobao Yuan on Longshan Mountain was one who knew he personally admired the Chan school. At the age of twenty-two, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He once took up his staff and traveled south, passing through Huxiang to visit the remains and traces of various patriarchs.

Initially, Daowu—whom the Master succeeded to—resided at Shichuang, a distance of one hundred and twenty li away. On the first and fifteenth days of every month, Zhiming would invariably walk there to pay homage at Daowu’s stupa, even in his old age.
It still did not stop. One night, there was a great thunderstorm, and the pagoda moved of its own accord to settle into its place.

To this day, it is called the "Thunder-Moved Pagoda. The Master then prostrated himself and composed a verse, saying: "A single thought of compassionate countenance is fundamentally never separated; why need one suddenly act so willfully and perversely?"
"Leveling the high and following the low, his compassionate heart was most earnest; he vexed the Thunder God into a night of busy toil. It was for this reason that the Master’s name was established.
Subsequently, he traveled to Shushan in Jiangxi, where Wen of Baiting and Lian of Huana both invited him to remain.
Not long after, he went to Zhejiang to see Wuyuan Quan at Tiantong and Xiuyan Rui, Kongsou Yin, and others at Maofeng. Yin held the position of *shiyuezhong* (the master who delights the assembly).
Subsequently, hearing of the reputation of Chan Master Pò'ān at Qiónglóng in Wúmén, he went there to rely upon him. Upon seeing him once, [Pò'ān] recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma.
In the meditation hall, when the master raised the story of the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Kāśyapa smiling, the master said: "A parched brick strikes and freezes through to the bottom;
a bloodshot eye bumps into a firebrand. Pò'ān secretly marveled at this, noting that [the master’s] words were present in every aspect of daily life.

[The Master] remained silent, thereby giving rise to [Wuzhun’s] doubts. The Master then resolved to rely upon him for refuge. At that time, he consulted with Wuzhun Fan daily, sharpening one another's resolve and vowing to satisfy the mind through practice.
Initially, after breaking his retreat at An, he moved to Zifu on Fengshan in Wuxing, where he appointed the Master as the Librarian (Zhizang).
One day, upon hearing that a saw was being used to split an iron weight, he experienced a sudden awakening; his long-standing doubts and obstructions dissolved completely.
Pō’ān once remarked, "These two men are fit to serve as 'seed-grass,'" referring specifically to the Master and Wǔzhǔn.

From then on, his reputation shone brightly throughout the monastic community. Not long after, when the Zīfú assembly dispersed, the Master traveled extensively to visit the gates of various elder masters, including Lín...
Yinsong Yuanjue, Jingci Kentang Chong, and Huazang Dun’an Yan were all said to have emerged from the forges of true masters;

thus, they were naturally exceptional. Later, when Daochang Fangqi was staying at Sujue, the abbot Wuchuan Zongzhi recognized his worth and invited him to share the teaching seat, whereupon the entire assembly submitted with joy.
Shortly thereafter, he appeared in the world at Gaohua Temple in Suzhou.

Fengbian Xiang brought forth [this case] for Pō’ān. Gaofeng’s small monastery was cramped and laborious; he led by personal example, and within three years, it had been transformed beyond recognition.
He subsequently moved to Fengqiao, where his followers were numerous and continuous. Among them were those of great virtue and high conduct.

Wuzu Fayan, Wushan Zhenjue, Wumen Huikai, and Shixi Daoyuan—these five or six men lived together in companionship, upholding and propagating the Dharma so that its reputation grew ever more magnificent.
When the seat at Zhongshan became vacant, the imperial court made a refined selection and appointed the Master to fill the position.
